When neither merge ran, `zcard` is called, but spans added by the Python zadd into set_key before the script are only counted via that fallback. The trimming relies on `zpopmin`, which drops the lowest scores (earliest end timestamps), so root or early spans can be dropped silently.

findings.title: Redirect loop depth limit reduced 10x without justification
findings.detail: The redirect-following loop limit dropped from 10000 to 1000, and the comment about the limit was deleted. Segment trees deeper than 1000 now silently fail to join, which is a behavioral regression unrelated to the sorted-set change.

findings.title: Span count guard removed from the flush path
findings.detail: The `max_segment_spans` check was removed from `_load_segment_data`, so oversized segments are no longer skipped when flushed. Only the Lua trim at 1000 enforces the limit, and the parameter `max_segment_spans` is now unused.

findings.title: Direct key access to end_timestamp_precise can crash the consumer
findings.detail: `val["end_timestamp_precise"]` raises KeyError if a span lacks the field, which fails the whole batch. Other optional fields use `.get`.

findings.title: Negative-offset pagination exposed to users via query param
findings.detail: A request parameter and cursor allow negative offsets, so Django queryset slicing is attempted with negative values. Django raises AssertionError on negative indexing, causing 500s. The comment claiming permissions are enforced at queryset level does not make this a safe boundary.

findings.title: Negative slice start passed to Django queryset
findings.detail: Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing and raise an AssertionError. The comment says the ORM handles negative slicing automatically, which is false. A crafted cursor such as 0:-5:1 causes an unhandled error, and the stop computation is wrong for negative starts.

findings.title: Base paginator still passes negative offset for prev cursors
findings.detail: The change in BasePaginator.get_result leaves offset unclamped when cursor.is_prev, so a user-supplied negative offset in a prev cursor reaches queryset slicing for all paginated endpoints. The comment claims negative offsets are safe, but they cause errors or wrong data. This also changes behavior for all endpoints using BasePaginator.
findings.evidence: start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset

findings.title: Redirect loop limit reduced 10x
findings.detail: The redirect-following loop was reduced from 10000 to 1000 iterations and the explanatory comment was removed. Deep segment trees will now not be joined correctly, silently splitting segments.

findings.title: Span count computed from partial merge and trimming drops newest spans
findings.detail: span_count is overwritten by the last zunionstore result, but that is the cardinality of set_key after the merge, so it is fine only if set_key merges happen; when the first merge is overwritten by the second this is still ok, but zpopmin removes the lowest scores, i.e. the earliest-ending spans, which may include the root/segment span. Also the cap is enforced only inside the Lua script, so spans added by the earlier zadd are trimmed silently with no metric.

findings.title: Segment span-count limit check removed
findings.detail: The max_segment_spans check and its metric and log were removed from _load_segment_data, while the SpansBuffer constructor still accepts max_segment_spans, now unused. Oversized segments are silently truncated by the Lua script instead of being reported.

findings.title: Required end_timestamp_precise accessed with direct indexing
findings.detail: A span payload missing end_timestamp_precise raises KeyError and crashes the entire batch processing, unlike parent_span_id which uses .get. The cast to SpanEvent only silences typing and does not validate input.

findings.title: Duplicated paginator with unused code and stale prev-trim logic
findings.detail: OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates BasePaginator.get_result; the prev-cursor trimming compares len(results) with offset + limit + extra using the raw (possibly negative) offset, which is inconsistent with the slice actually used.

findings.title: Privileged paginator with negative offsets exposed via query param
findings.detail: Any user with global access can pass `optimized_pagination=true` and a crafted cursor with a negative offset to reach the new negative-slicing path. The comment 'permissions are checked at the queryset level' does not make this safe.

findings.title: Negative slicing on Django QuerySet raises error
findings.detail: Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing; `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start raises AssertionError ('Negative indexing is not supported'). A user-supplied cursor offset such as -5 therefore causes a 500 on the optimized path.

findings.title: Prev-cursor offset is not clamped, so negative offsets reach the queryset in the base paginator
findings.detail: The change only clamps for non-prev cursors. With `is_prev` set, a negative offset from a client cursor passes through unchanged into `queryset[...]`, which raises an error. The comment claims negative offsets are allowed and handled, and this is inconsistent with the clamp and the actual behaviour.
findings.evidence: start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset

findings.title: Prev-cursor trimming uses the raw offset instead of the slice start
findings.detail: For the is_prev case, the check `len(results) == offset + limit + extra` assumes the slice starts at the raw offset. If the offset is clamped or negative the result length no longer matches, so the extra row is not dropped.

findings.title: Trimming a segment with zpopmin discards the oldest spans
findings.detail: When a segment exceeds 1000 spans the script silently removes the lowest-scored (earliest-ending) spans, so the segment loses data. This replaces the previous behaviour of skipping an oversized segment, and the `max_segment_spans` check was removed from the consumer.

findings.title: span_count is overwritten rather than accumulated
findings.detail: The two zunionstore calls each assign span_count, so only the last result is kept. That is the correct size of set_key after the second merge, but it is stale if the second branch does not run. A non-trivial interplay with the later `span_count == 0` fallback means the trimming condition depends on branch order.

findings.title: Redirect loop limit reduced 10x without justification
findings.detail: Reducing the loop bound from 10000 to 1000 means deep segment trees will no longer be joined correctly, and the explanatory comment was removed. This change is unrelated to the zset migration.

findings.title: Required end_timestamp_precise read with direct indexing
findings.detail: Spans lacking `end_timestamp_precise` raise KeyError and crash the whole batch. Other optional fields are read with .get(), and `cast` provides no runtime validation.

findings.title: Span count limit enforcement removed from flush path
findings.detail: The `max_segment_spans` check in `_load_segment_data` was removed, leaving the parameter unused. Enforcement now depends only on the Lua trim, which drops data rather than skipping oversized segments.

findings.title: Cache key uses non-deterministic hash() of project ids
findings.detail: Python's hash() of a tuple of ints is stable, but the key ignores the allowlist contents, so the cached eligibility goes stale for 60s after allowlist changes. The cache is also unnecessary for an in-memory option lookup, and it breaks tests that mock options (a cached True/False from one test leaks into the next).

findings.title: Dataset checked against wrong object; wrapper discover dataset vs request.GET query
findings.detail: Upsampling in discover is decided by the substring 'event.type:error' in the raw request query, but _get_event_stats is also called with modified queries (e.g. '!event.type:transaction' splits) and scoped_dataset, while the code passes the outer `dataset`. Queries like '!event.type:error' or 'event.type:error_foo' match the substring and get upsampled incorrectly, while split-dashboard error queries are not upsampled.

findings.title: Eligibility check uses outer dataset instead of scoped_dataset
findings.detail: is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects is called with the closure `dataset` rather than the `scoped_dataset` argument that actually executes the query. For dashboard split paths (scoped_dataset=discover with an error-only query) the decision is made on the wrong dataset, so upsampling is applied or skipped incorrectly.

findings.title: Only exact 'count()' is transformed; aliases and other aggregates ignored
findings.detail: Only the literal column 'count()' is rewritten, so other aggregations (e.g., eps(), epm(), count_unique) remain un-upsampled. Output also aliases to 'count', which can collide with a requested column and alters transform_alias_to_input_format behavior (result key becomes 'count' not 'count()').

findings.title: upsampled_count sums sample_weight that may be NULL/absent
findings.detail: The aggregate sums sample_weight with no handling of NULL or missing values (events without client sample rate), so such events contribute 0 instead of 1, undercounting. The comments claim the column always exists, which is not enforced.

findings.title: Falsy check and blanket exception swallowing in sample rate helper
findings.detail: `if client_sample_rate:` skips a valid 0 value, and bare `except Exception: pass` silently hides malformed contexts. The helper also sets the 'sample_rate' field on event data in test factories only, making production behavior untested.

findings.title: Upsampling test depends on weight that is never set via real ingest
findings.detail: The test asserts count == 10, which relies on a test-only factory hack deriving sample_rate from the context; also it does not invalidate the 60s cache between tests, so mocked options may be bypassed by a cached eligibility value for the same project ids.
findings.evidence: assert data[0][1][0]["count"] == 10  # First bucket has 1 event

findings.title: Stray git submodule added
findings.detail: An unrelated submodule pointer 'sentry-repo' is committed, which is likely accidental and breaks checkouts without the submodule configured.

findings.title: Cache key uses Python hash() of project IDs, which is not stable or unique
findings.detail: hash() of a tuple is process-dependent and can collide, so different project sets may share a cache entry and workers may disagree. A collision could make a non-allowlisted project set be upsampled. Use the joined IDs (or a stable digest) as the key.

findings.title: Allowlist cache is never invalidated and contradicts the 'always latest' docstring
findings.detail: Eligibility is cached for 60s and invalidate_upsampling_cache is never called when the option changes. Stale results are served. The docstring of _are_all_projects_error_upsampled claims fresh reads are intentional, which is contradicted by this cache.

findings.title: Error-focused detection is a naive substring match on the raw query
findings.detail: Substring check on 'event.type:error' matches negations like '!event.type:error' or compound queries mixing event types, causing upsampling to be applied to non-error data. The dashboard split path issues queries like '(q) AND !event.type:transaction' that are not recognized, so behavior is inconsistent. The check reads the request query, not the actual query passed to _get_event_stats.

findings.title: Eligibility check uses outer `dataset` rather than `scoped_dataset`
findings.detail: _get_event_stats is called with different scoped datasets (e.g. discover for the split-widget path), but the upsampling decision is computed against the closed-over `dataset`. Upsampling can be applied or skipped for the wrong dataset.

findings.title: Only count() is transformed; other aggregates and RPC datasets are mishandled
findings.detail: For RPC datasets such as spans_rpc/ourlogs, the eligibility returns False via the dataset check, but for errors/discover the 'upsampled_count() as count' alias form may not be supported by every path (e.g. top events with transform_alias_to_input_format). Other aggregates such as eps()/epm() are not upsampled, giving inconsistent numbers.

findings.title: upsampled_count sums sample_weight with no null/zero handling
findings.detail: Events lacking sample_weight (the column is nullable) contribute null/0 so the upsampled count would undercount them instead of counting them as 1. The code comments assume the column exists for all events, which is not guaranteed.

findings.title: Broad swallowed exceptions in test factory helper
findings.detail: Bare 'except Exception: pass' hides malformed contexts, and a falsy check skips valid values. Failures to set sample_rate silently produce wrong test data.

findings.title: Accidental submodule pointer added
findings.detail: A gitlink for 'sentry-repo' pointing at an unrelated commit is added to the repository, which is almost certainly accidental and unrelated to this change.

findings.title: Tests mock the whole options module
findings.detail: Patching 'options' in the helper makes options.get return the same list for any key, and the cache is not cleared between tests, so results with the same org/project key may leak across tests within 60s. The assertions can pass or fail depending on cached state.

findings.title: Cache key uses Python hash(); stale and collision-prone, never invalidated
findings.detail: The key uses built-in hash() of a tuple of project ids. This is not a stable identifier and can collide, so one project set may read another set's cached eligibility. invalidate_upsampling_cache is never called, so allowlist changes stay stale for 60s. Caching a cheap options.get also contradicts the 'always latest configuration' note in _are_all_projects_error_upsampled.

findings.title: Upsampling check uses outer `dataset` instead of `scoped_dataset`; query string not used
findings.detail: Eligibility is computed against the closed-over `dataset`, not the `scoped_dataset` being queried. Dashboard split-widget paths call _get_event_stats with `discover` or different datasets, so the transform may be applied to the wrong dataset. For discover it also inspects request.GET['query'] rather than the actual `query` argument (which gets '!event.type:transaction' appended), so transforms can hit transaction queries where sample_weight doesn't exist.

findings.title: Error-focused detection is a naive substring match
findings.detail: `"event.type:error" in query` also matches `!event.type:error`, `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction`, and `event.type:errors...`. This wrongly enables upsampling for queries that include non-error events or negation.

findings.title: Only exact 'count()' is transformed, aliases/other aggregates ignored
findings.detail: Only the literal string count() is rewritten. Equivalent forms such as 'count() as x' or equations/other count-based functions stay un-upsampled, giving inconsistent results. Also the transform forces alias 'count', which may break callers expecting the original column name.

findings.title: upsampled_count sums sample_weight that may be NULL/absent
findings.detail: The aggregate assumes sample_weight is populated for all events. For events without it, sum() skips them and returns 0 or too small a count, silently undercounting; the code makes no coalesce/fallback to 1. Also the declared result type 'number' while casting to Int64 is inconsistent.

findings.title: Test setUp overwrites self.user after use and tests assert magic counts
findings.detail: self.user is replaced by a new user after login, making authed_user confusing; assertions of exactly 10 depend on the testutils factory hack that sets sample_rate from context. Also the new unit test never covers is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects or the cache path, which is where the bug lies.

findings.title: Blanket exception swallowing hides invalid data
findings.detail: Broad `except Exception: pass` blocks hide malformed contexts, and the truthiness check skips a legitimate rate of 0; tests silently run without sample_rate.

findings.title: Stray submodule commit added
findings.detail: An unrelated git submodule entry 'sentry-repo' is added to the repository, which is not part of the feature.

findings.title: Call to nonexistent no-arg isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()
findings.detail: The only definition is `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` in UsernamePasswordForm. The no-arg call does not compile, so the services module fails to build.

findings.title: Passkeys disabled when no user is identified yet
findings.detail: The helper requires `user != null`, but the passkeys setup was previously done precisely when the user was null. Now `authenticate()` and `challenge()` skip `fillContextForm` on the initial login page and after username errors, so conditional UI is lost for normal logins. The existing tests that expect the webauthn form on the first page would fail.

findings.title: retryCount delete clause not restricted to SMS reminders
findings.detail: The second OR branch has no `method: SMS` condition, so it deletes any WorkflowReminder (EMAIL, WHATSAPP) with retryCount > 1. The SMS cron handler can therefore remove other methods' reminders, and the column is shared with other flows.

findings.title: Off-by-one in retry threshold: `gt: 1` allows only 2 attempts
findings.detail: Reminders are deleted when retryCount > 1, so a reminder is deleted after just two failures and the retry count is effectively 2. Also, deletion of the row on repeated failure silently drops the reminder without any record.

findings.title: Unguarded DB update inside catch block can abort the whole loop
findings.detail: The retryCount update in the catch block is not wrapped in its own try/catch. If the update fails (e.g., DB error or the row was deleted/not found), it throws out of the loop and the handler, skipping all remaining reminders and returning a 500.

findings.title: Retry increment only on falsy scheduledSMS; not when message/sendTo is missing
findings.detail: When the message is empty or sendTo is missing, nothing increments retryCount, so such reminders are retried forever on each cron run. Also the else branch increments from a stale in-memory value rather than atomically (`increment`).

findings.title: retryCount cleanup is not limited to SMS reminders
findings.detail: The second OR branch has no `method: SMS` condition, so this SMS cron handler deletes any WorkflowReminder (EMAIL, WHATSAPP) whose retryCount > 1. Reminders of other methods can be destroyed by a handler that should only touch SMS.

findings.title: Off-by-one: reminders deleted after only two failed attempts
findings.detail: The filter `retryCount: { gt: 1 }` deletes a reminder once retryCount reaches 2, so a reminder gets only 2 attempts. The cleanup runs before the fetch, and a reminder at retryCount 1 that fails again is incremented to 2, then deleted on the next run. This is likely stricter than the intended retry limit, and the limit is hardcoded.

findings.title: Retry-count update in catch block can itself throw
findings.detail: The prisma update inside the catch is not guarded. If the DB call fails, the exception escapes the loop, aborts processing of all remaining reminders, and results in a 500 response. The original error is also never logged.

findings.title: Non-atomic retryCount increment based on stale value
findings.detail: Retry count is written as `reminder.retryCount + 1` from a value read earlier rather than via Prisma's `{ increment: 1 }`. Overlapping cron runs can lose increments, so the retry limit is not enforced reliably.

findings.title: retryCount cleanup is not limited to SMS reminders and deletes other methods
findings.detail: The second OR branch has no `method: SMS` condition, so any WorkflowReminder (EMAIL or WHATSAPP) with retryCount > 1 is deleted by the SMS cron. Other reminder types sharing the table can be lost.

findings.title: Off-by-one: retryCount > 1 allows only two attempts and deletes the reminder
findings.detail: A reminder is deleted once retryCount exceeds 1, so it is retried only twice before being removed. Deletion also discards the reminder entirely, so a failed SMS is silently dropped with no record. The threshold also looks inconsistent with typical retry limits (e.g. gt 2 for 3 tries).

findings.title: Update in catch block can throw and abort the whole loop
findings.detail: The prisma.workflowReminder.update inside the catch is not guarded; if it fails (e.g. DB error or the row was deleted), the exception escapes the loop, stops processing remaining reminders and returns a 500. The original error is also never logged because console.log comes after the update.

findings.title: Retry count is incremented even when the failure happened after a successful schedule
findings.detail: The catch increments retryCount for any exception, including one thrown by the prisma update that follows a successful twilio.scheduleSMS call. The SMS is already scheduled but the reminder stays unscheduled and may be scheduled again, producing duplicate SMS. The retry count also gets bumped for permanent data errors, e.g. a missing attendee.

findings.title: Non-atomic retryCount increment based on stale value
findings.detail: The new count is computed from the previously read value (`reminder.retryCount + 1`) rather than using Prisma's atomic `{ increment: 1 }`. Concurrent cron runs can overwrite each other and undercount retries.

findings.title: Team admin check uses AND instead of OR

findings.title: Email failure is swallowed with no error detail

findings.title: Calendar update runs with the caller's credentials, not the organizer's

findings.title: Error toast message is never empty and shows raw code

findings.title: Subject uses first attendee name, which may be empty

findings.title: Team admin check uses AND instead of OR
findings.detail: Requiring the user to be both team admin AND team owner is wrong: admins who are not owners are denied, and the combined check is meaningless. Team admins or owners should pass.

findings.title: Any attendee may add guests to a booking
findings.detail: Authorization lets any attendee (matched by email only) modify the booking and add guests, who then receive emails and calendar invites. The email match is also case-sensitive and unverified, so permission is both too broad and fragile.

findings.title: New guests get scheduled email, existing attendees get add-guests email
findings.detail: The branch is inverted relative to its intent: new guests receive the generic AttendeeScheduledEmail while existing attendees (who already knew the event) get the 'guests added' notification. Also uses exact string match so case differences break the split.

findings.title: Emails sent with the unfiltered guest list
findings.detail: sendAddGuestsEmails is passed the raw input guests instead of uniqueGuests, so blacklisted or already-existing attendees are treated as new guests when deciding which email template to use.

findings.title: Case-sensitive blacklist and duplicate comparison
findings.detail: Blacklist entries are lowercased but the guest email is not, so mixed-case emails bypass the blacklist. Duplicate check against existing attendees is also case-sensitive, and duplicates within the input are not removed server-side.

findings.title: Calendar update not guarded and email errors swallowed

findings.title: Calendar credentials taken from the acting user, not the organizer

findings.title: Error toast message is never falsy and shows raw code

findings.title: Any attendee can add guests to the booking
findings.detail: Authorization allows any existing attendee (matched by email) to add guests. Attendees are untrusted third parties, and an attendee can invite arbitrary people and trigger emails and calendar updates. Matching by an unverified email string also weakens the check.

findings.title: Blacklist and duplicate checks are case-sensitive and skip normalization
findings.detail: The blacklist is lowercased but the guest email is compared as-is, so 'Foo@X.com' bypasses the blacklist. Duplicate detection against existing attendees is also case-sensitive, and duplicate guests within the input are not deduplicated server-side.

findings.title: Email templates swapped: new guests get 'scheduled', existing get 'guests added'

findings.title: Email failure swallowed without logging the error

findings.title: Calendar update uses the caller's credentials and event manager rather than the organizer's

Other consumers of getCalendarCredentials that use `.calendar` directly (not via the updated getConnectedCalendars) will call methods on a Promise and fail. The return type of the function silently changes.

findings.title: Async forEach callback pushes to apiDeletes after it has been awaited
findings.detail: The forEach callback is async and now awaits getCalendar before deleting events, so the handler continues past it and runs `Promise.all(apiDeletes)` before the deletes are pushed. Recurring calendar events may not be deleted before the request returns, and errors become unhandled rejections.

findings.title: async forEach makes calendar/video deletes fire-and-forget; try/catch ineffective
findings.detail: Using an async callback in forEach means returned promises are discarded. Errors from getCalendar or deleteEvent are no longer caught by the surrounding try/catch and become unhandled rejections, and the deletions may not finish before the function returns.

findings.title: async forEach makes calendar/video deletes fire-and-forget; try/catch ineffective
findings.detail: Same issue: the async forEach callback is not awaited, so deletions are not awaited and errors escape the try/catch as unhandled rejections.

findings.title: async forEach in reschedule request not awaited
findings.detail: The async forEach callback is not awaited, so calendar deletions can still be running after the mutation proceeds. Failures become unhandled rejections instead of surfacing to the caller.

findings.title: All app modules are imported eagerly at module load via import() in object literal
findings.detail: Each `import(...)` runs immediately when the object is created, so all apps are still loaded at startup (now as unawaited promises), defeating lazy loading. A failing import also becomes an unhandled rejection at module load, and every consumer must now await the value.

findings.title: Warning logs the awaited module/undefined instead of app name
findings.detail: Now that paymentApp is the awaited module namespace, the warning message interpolates `${paymentApp}` which prints `[object Module]` or undefined, giving a useless message.
findings.evidence: const paymentApp = await appStore[paymentAppCredential?.app?.dirName as keyof typeof appStore];

findings.title: Sequential awaits in getVideoAdapters loop
findings.detail: Adapters are resolved serially in a for loop with await, adding latency when multiple credentials are passed (e.g. getBusyVideoTimes) compared to the previous synchronous reduce.
findings.evidence: const app = await appStore[appName as keyof typeof appStore];

findings.title: Email reminders with referenceId are never deleted on cancel; only flagged
findings.detail: For scheduled email reminders without immediateDelete, the function only sets cancelled=true and never cancels the SendGrid batch. The cron job only picks up cancelled reminders within 1 hour of scheduledDate, but emails scheduled up to 72h out are already queued in SendGrid. The earlier cron step also deletes past-due reminders, so a cancelled reminder may be removed before the batch is ever cancelled and the email is still sent.

findings.title: Cancelled reminders found without filtering by method or null referenceId
findings.detail: The query selects all cancelled reminders regardless of method or referenceId, then posts to SendGrid with batch_id possibly null. A single failure inside the loop aborts the try block, leaving all remaining cancelled reminders unprocessed.

findings.title: Cancelled reminders can be rescheduled by the unscheduled-reminder step
findings.detail: The unscheduled reminder query does not exclude cancelled=true. Cancelled reminders with scheduled:false and referenceId null are deleted immediately for that case, but a cancelled reminder with scheduled=true is untouched, and any cancelled one in the cron window can still be processed and sent.

findings.title: try/catch around async delete calls does not catch rejections
findings.detail: The delete functions are async and not awaited inside forEach, so the try/catch cannot catch their errors. They run concurrently without being awaited and may not finish before the request ends.

findings.title: Reschedule uses immediateDelete for email but never removes DB reminder rows
findings.detail: With immediateDelete=true and a referenceId, the email batch is cancelled but the WorkflowReminder row is neither deleted nor flagged. Stale rows persist, and the old fire-and-forget approach was replaced inconsistently with the SMS path, which deletes the row.

findings.title: Deleted-step and deleted-workflow reminders keep DB rows after immediate email cancel
findings.detail: With immediateDelete=true, the email path cancels the SendGrid batch and returns without deleting the DB row. Reminders for deleted workflows or steps rely on cascade delete only in some cases and are left orphaned in others.

findings.title: Edited-step reminders are no longer deleted and async forEach removes ownership check
findings.detail: The prior deleteMany with a booking.userId ownership filter was removed in favor of unawaited per-reminder deletion. The async forEach is not awaited so subsequent regeneration of reminders may race with the deletes.

findings.title: Value imports of types and unformatted import
findings.detail: PrismaPromise and Prisma are now imported as runtime values although they are only used as types, and the last import lacks a trailing comma. Also, the diff re-indents a commented-out block, causing noise.

findings.title: Runtime imports of types from @prisma/client
findings.detail: App, Credential, EventTypeCustomInput and Prisma are types, but were changed from type-only imports to value imports. This can break under isolatedModules or bundlers that cannot elide them.

findings.title: Sender ID block removed from conditional
findings.detail: Condition changed from (isPhoneNumberNeeded || isSenderIdNeeded) to only isPhoneNumberNeeded and the unrelated UI refactor adds risk without relation to the PR purpose.

findings.title: Email reminders with a referenceId are never cancelled at the provider unless immediateDelete
findings.detail: Without immediateDelete, an email reminder that has a referenceId is only flagged cancelled=true in the DB. SendGrid is cancelled later, only by the cron, and only for reminders due within 1 hour. A reminder already scheduled in SendGrid for sooner than that (the scheduling window is 72h) can be sent before the cron runs. Cancelled and rescheduled bookings can therefore still send the email.

findings.title: immediateDelete cancels in SendGrid but never deletes the DB row
findings.detail: On the immediateDelete path, the batch is cancelled at SendGrid and then the function returns. The WorkflowReminder row is never deleted. Callers such as workflow deletion, step removal and reschedule in handleNewBooking rely on the row being removed, and the old code deleted it. Stale rows stay behind, and the old DELETE of the scheduled send is no longer made.

findings.title: Cron query for cancelled reminders is unscoped and one failure aborts the batch
findings.detail: The findMany filters only on cancelled and scheduledDate, with no method filter, and has no lower bound on scheduledDate. The loop is inside a single try block, so one failed SendGrid request stops the rest of the batch. The deletes are created lazily and only awaited at the end, so the rows of reminders already cancelled at SendGrid are never deleted when a later request throws. Meanwhile the earlier deleteMany removes past-due EMAIL reminders without the cancelled flag being considered.

findings.title: try/catch around async reminder deletions cannot catch their errors
findings.detail: deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are async and are not awaited inside forEach. The surrounding try/catch therefore catches nothing from them, and the deletions run unawaited while the reschedule continues. A later failure leaves reminders in an undefined state.

findings.title: Async reminder cancellation is fire-and-forget, racing with later operations
findings.detail: The delete/cancel calls are no longer awaited, and the DB deletes they replaced used to be awaited. The mutation proceeds to recreate or schedule reminders for the same bookings while these calls are still running. Errors are swallowed and the request can finish before cancellation completes. The `remindersToUpdate.forEach(async ...)` wrapper is now pointless.

findings.title: Reminders no longer awaited on cancel; unscheduled or SMS state may be lost
findings.detail: Reminder cancellation is fired without awaiting and is excluded from prismaPromises, so the handler can return before cancellation finishes. Errors are only logged. The old code awaited the DB deletes together with the other deletes.

findings.title: Removed ownership check on reminder deletion
findings.detail: The previous deleteMany scoped deletion to reminders whose booking.userId was ctx.user.id. The new helper deletes or updates purely by reminder id with no ownership condition.

findings.title: Unrelated reindentation of commented-out code strips formatting
findings.detail: The commented-out testAction block was reindented to flush-left. This is noise unrelated to the change, and it also dropped the trailing comma after `Prisma` in the import list.

findings.title: Email reminders already scheduled in SendGrid are not cancelled on cancel/disable
findings.detail: When immediateDelete is false (cancelled bookings, edited steps, disabled event types), the function only flags `cancelled: true` and returns. SendGrid is only told to cancel via the cron, and only for reminders due within the next hour. Reminders scheduled further out can still go out, and the cron's own cleanup `deleteMany` removes any reminder whose scheduledDate has passed, so the DB row may be deleted before the batch is cancelled.

findings.title: Cancel query not restricted to EMAIL method and may include rows without referenceId
findings.detail: findMany filters only on cancelled and scheduledDate, not on method EMAIL or a non-null referenceId. A reminder with a null referenceId, or a non-email reminder, would be sent to SendGrid as batch_id null and make the request throw. Because the try block wraps the whole loop, one failure aborts all remaining cancellations and deletions.

findings.title: Single failure aborts all pending cancellations
findings.detail: The sequential awaited SendGrid requests are in one try/catch, and the prisma delete promises are only awaited after the loop. If one request fails, the loop exits, the already-created delete queries are never awaited, and the remaining reminders stay uncancelled. The error is only logged.

findings.title: immediateDelete path cancels in SendGrid but never removes the DB row
findings.detail: With immediateDelete=true and a referenceId, the batch is cancelled in SendGrid and the function returns without deleting the workflowReminder row. Callers such as workflow deletion and removed steps rely on this path, so orphaned reminder rows stay behind. The old code did a SendGrid DELETE and the callers deleted rows explicitly.

findings.title: Edited-step reminders marked cancelled rather than removed, with async forEach and no awaiting
findings.detail: The reminder cleanup functions are async but are called without await in forEach (and in an async callback). The following code that recreates reminders for the edited steps can run before the cancel flag or delete is written, and errors are only swallowed.

findings.title: Reminder cleanup is not awaited and was removed from the awaited promise set
findings.detail: The delete/cancel calls return promises that are neither awaited nor added to prismaPromises. The handler can return before they finish, which in serverless environments can drop the work. Rejections are only logged inside the helpers.

findings.title: Ownership check dropped when deleting reminders for disabled event types
findings.detail: The old code deleted reminders only where booking.userId matched ctx.user.id. The new code deletes every reminder by id with no such constraint, relying solely on how remindersToDelete was queried upstream.

findings.title: Unrelated whitespace edits inside a commented-out block corrupt indentation
findings.detail: The diff changes the indentation of the commented-out testAction code, stripping leading whitespace for no functional reason.

findings.title: Default `queued` timestamp evaluated once at import time
findings.detail: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once when the class is defined, so every AssignmentSource shares the same stale timestamp. It should use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`.

findings.detail: `to_dict()` uses `asdict`, which leaves `queued` as a datetime object. It is passed in `apply_async` kwargs, and JSON serializers may fail or turn it into a string. `from_dict` then passes that string to the constructor without parsing it back.

findings.title: New `assignment_source` kwarg passed to all integrations' sync_assignee_outbound
findings.detail: The task now always passes `assignment_source=...` to `installation.sync_assignee_outbound`. The abstract signature only has `**kwargs`, but implementations that don't accept extra kwargs would raise TypeError. The sync_status_outbound signature was also changed without any caller using it.

findings.title: Cycle prevention compares against the wrong ID semantics and is not applied to inbound checks
findings.detail: The check in `should_sync` is a no-op for other callers such as `where_should_sync`, which calls `should_sync(key)` with no source. Only the outbound assignee task is protected. Status sync and any subclass overriding `should_sync` with the old signature will break when called with the second positional argument.

findings.title: to_dict test cannot catch import-time default or serialization issues
findings.detail: The test only checks that `queued` is not None, which passes with the frozen import-time default. There is no round-trip test (to_dict then from_dict), so the datetime serialization problem is not caught.

findings.title: Default `queued` timestamp evaluated once at import time
findings.detail: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once when the class is defined, so every AssignmentSource gets the same stale timestamp rather than its creation time. It should use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`.

findings.title: to_dict yields a datetime that is not JSON-serializable for the Celery task
findings.detail: `asdict` keeps `queued` as a datetime object. The dict is passed in `apply_async` kwargs, so a JSON serializer will fail or convert it to a string. On the receiving side `from_dict` then builds the object with a string `queued` instead of a datetime.

findings.title: Failed parsing of the assignment source is silently swallowed
findings.detail: `from_dict` returns None on a malformed dict, and the task then treats it as no source. The cycle-prevention check is skipped without any log, so a sync loop can reappear unnoticed.

findings.title: New assignment_source kwarg passed to all installations' sync_assignee_outbound
findings.detail: `assignment_source=` is now passed to every integration's `sync_assignee_outbound`. Implementations that do not accept `**kwargs` (including the abstract signature's subclasses) would raise TypeError. The abstract `sync_assignee_outbound` was not updated to declare the parameter.

findings.title: Source check applies to every sync attribute, not just assignee
findings.detail: The sync-source check in `should_sync` returns False for any attribute, including status and comments, when the source integration matches. `sync_source` is typed as AssignmentSource and documented for assignment, so this could unintentionally block other sync types if a source is passed.

findings.title: Default `queued` timestamp is evaluated once at import time
findings.detail: `timezone.now()` as a dataclass default runs once when the module loads, so every AssignmentSource shares the same stale timestamp rather than its creation time. The `queued` field is therefore meaningless.

findings.title: to_dict result contains a datetime that is not JSON-serializable for the task queue
findings.detail: `asdict` returns `queued` as a datetime object. The dict is passed as a kwarg to `apply_async`, so a JSON serializer will fail or convert it to a string. After conversion `from_dict` would hand a string to `queued`, which has no validation.

findings.title: Invalid assignment source silently disables sync-cycle protection
findings.detail: `from_dict` returns None on a malformed dict, and the task treats that the same as 'no source'. The outbound sync then proceeds, which can reintroduce the sync loop this change prevents. The failure is also not logged.

findings.title: Abstract sync_status_outbound signature changed, but sync_assignee_outbound still lacks assignment_source
findings.detail: The task now passes `assignment_source=` to `installation.sync_assignee_outbound`. The abstract signature has only `**kwargs`, so implementations without `**kwargs` will raise TypeError. Meanwhile the unrelated `sync_status_outbound` gains an `assignment_source` parameter that nothing passes.

findings.title: Cycle check applies to all attributes, including inbound and status
findings.detail: The integration_id comparison is not restricted to outbound assignee sync. A call to `should_sync` with any attribute and a matching source returns False, which is broader than the comment describes.

findings.title: Offset tracker skips gaps in offsets and commits past unprocessed messages
findings.detail: get_committable_offsets stops at the first offset missing from all_offsets. After mark_committed prunes entries, a later poll starts from last_committed+1, so any offset not yet submitted is treated as a gap that blocks. Conversely, Kafka offsets are naturally non-contiguous (compaction, transaction markers), so commits stall forever on the first gap. The inverse problem is also real: in-flight offsets that were submitted later than a completed one are tracked only once submitted.

findings.title: Worker shutdown flag drops queued items; offsets never completed
findings.detail: `shutdown` is set to True before queues are shut down. A worker that finishes its current item exits the loop without draining remaining queued items (and `shutdown` also shadows the Thread API name). Those items never run and their offsets stay outstanding, which contradicts the 'graceful' docstring.

findings.title: queue.ShutDown / Queue.shutdown only exist in Python 3.13+
findings.detail: `queue.ShutDown` and `Queue.shutdown()` were added in Python 3.13. On older runtimes, the `except queue.ShutDown` clause raises AttributeError when evaluated, and `q.shutdown` fails. Workers would then never be unblocked from the blocking `get()`.

findings.title: Exit path after ShutDown inside processing skips nothing but loses remaining work
findings.detail: `except queue.ShutDown: break` inside the processing block exits the worker; also `get()` blocks indefinitely when `shutdown` flag is set while idle and the queue is never shut down by the flag alone. A hang until the queue is shut down and join timeouts after 5s per worker can make shutdown take num_queues*5s.

findings.title: hash() of str is randomized per process, breaking group affinity
findings.detail: Python string hashing is salted per process (PYTHONHASHSEED), so the same subscription maps to different queues across consumer processes/restarts. Ordering is only guaranteed within one process; docstring claims 'consistent hashing'. Use a stable hash (e.g. crc32).

findings.title: Committable offset logic skips unseen offsets and commits across gaps/partition revocation
findings.detail: Commit state is tied to the pool, which is shared across all strategy instances created per rebalance; the strategy's commit thread and offset tracker are never reset on rebalance, so stale offsets for revoked partitions can be committed. Also the loop starts at min_offset when last_committed is -1, so a gap before the first seen offset is treated as committed, and the tracker is shared by multiple strategies.

findings.title: Lock creation and defaultdict access not thread-safe
findings.detail: `get_committable_offsets` iterates `list(self.all_offsets.keys())` while other threads insert into defaultdicts without a global lock. `_get_partition_lock` uses setdefault which is fine, but defaultdict insertion of new partitions occurs under different per-partition locks, which is racy with the commit thread.

findings.title: Submit failure marks offset completed, causing silent message loss
findings.detail: On any exception during submit (e.g. grouping_fn error), the offset is marked completed and will be committed, dropping the message. Also, if the exception happens after `add_offset` in pool.submit, it's re-added harmlessly, but the message is still lost.

findings.title: Commit loop runs a final pass only after waiting; no final commit on close
findings.detail: close() sets the shutdown event and joins the commit thread without a final commit of completed offsets, and queue_pool.shutdown happens after the join. Completed offsets since the last tick are not committed, causing reprocessing. Also no backpressure exists despite the docstring claiming it (unbounded queues).

findings.title: Error-handling test asserts nothing useful about commits
findings.detail: The test is titled 'errors don't block offset commits' but asserts no commit for the partition occurs; the ResultProcessor swallows exceptions in practice, and the assertion is vacuous/contradicts the docstring.
findings.evidence: assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets

findings.title: Distribution test depends on randomized string hash
findings.detail: Asserting all 3 queues are hit by 20 hashed keys is non-deterministic across processes due to hash randomization (small flake probability).

findings.title: Commit thread and worker threads share a queue pool across strategy instances
findings.detail: The queue pool and its OffsetTracker are owned by the factory and shared by every strategy created via create_with_partitions. On a rebalance, the old strategy's close() calls queue_pool.shutdown(), which shuts down the queues and workers, so the newly created strategy submits to a dead pool. Offsets from revoked partitions also stay in the shared tracker and can be committed for partitions no longer assigned.

findings.title: Committable offset logic breaks on non-contiguous Kafka offsets and loses data on gaps
findings.detail: Offsets are treated as contiguous integers, so any gap in the offset sequence (compaction, transaction markers, filtered messages) stops commits forever at the gap. Once all_offsets is pruned, `offset in all_offsets` fails for a missing offset, so the loop breaks at that offset even though nothing is outstanding. The commit can then stall permanently and the consumer reprocesses everything after a restart.

findings.title: Lost-update race between commit and in-flight add_offset when last_committed is unset
findings.detail: If the commit loop calls mark_committed after committing but new offsets were added meanwhile, this is fine. However, get_committable_offsets iterates `list(self.all_offsets.keys())` while submit mutates the defaultdict, and `self.all_offsets[partition]` with defaultdict creates entries without a lock. The unlocked creation and the lock-free `partition_locks.get` rely on GIL luck. The first check-then-set on locks is OK but the defaultdicts are mutated outside any global lock.

findings.title: Worker exits on shutdown flag without draining remaining queued items; flag checked only between gets
findings.detail: shutdown() sets worker.shutdown=True and then shuts down queues with immediate=False. A worker that finishes an item sees shutdown True and exits immediately, leaving queued items unprocessed, so the 'gracefully shutdown' docstring is false. Those offsets stay outstanding and are never committed, so they are reprocessed after a restart.

findings.title: queue.ShutDown and Queue.shutdown require Python 3.13
findings.detail: queue.ShutDown and Queue.shutdown() only exist in Python 3.13+. On older runtimes, evaluating the `except queue.ShutDown` clause raises AttributeError, and q.shutdown fails for every queue.

findings.title: Failed submit is marked completed and committed, silently dropping messages
findings.detail: On any exception during submit (including queue put failures) the offset is added and immediately completed, so it becomes committable and the message is lost. The class docstring claims offsets are committed only after successful processing.

findings.title: hash(str) is randomized per process, so group-to-queue assignment is not stable
findings.detail: Python's string hash is salted per process (PYTHONHASHSEED). Assignment is consistent within one process, but the docstring promises 'consistent hashing'. The mapping is not meaningful across restarts or processes, which matters if ordering is expected across consumers.

findings.title: Commit loop never performs a final commit on close, and a worker that breaks on ShutDown leaves the finally referencing work_item
findings.detail: close() sets the shutdown event and the commit loop wakes from wait and still runs one more commit pass, but terminated workers leave outstanding offsets so they are never committed. Also backpressure is claimed ('Natural backpressure when queues fill up') but the queues are unbounded, so submit never blocks and memory grows without limit.
findings.evidence: - Natural backpressure when queues fill up

findings.title: Error-handling test asserts nothing about commits for the failing message
findings.detail: The assertion `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` contradicts the docstring that errors do not block commits. Also, ResultProcessor.__call__ is patched with a side_effect exception, which is swallowed by the worker, and the test asserts that no commit occurs. This cannot catch a regression where errored messages are never committed.
