findings.detail: `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` is read directly, but `build_integration` only stores `sender` when `state.get("sender")` is truthy. Integrations created without it (including existing ones) raise KeyError and the installation fails with a 500.

findings.title: OAuth state is a static pipeline signature, not a per-request nonce
findings.detail: The OAuth `state` is `pipeline.signature`, which is deterministic and reused. It is not random and not bound to the user session, so it gives weak CSRF protection for the OAuth callback. The state is also sent unencoded in the URL.

findings.title: Installation-id fallback to the pipeline state can be reached without the `installation_id` param
findings.detail: `request.GET.get("installation_id", pipeline.fetch_state(...))` only falls back when the key is absent. Because OAuthLoginView binds the installation_id from the first request, the later step proceeds using state alone. Combined with the 'sender' comparison being skipped when no Integration exists, a first-time install performs no check that the authenticated user owns the installation.

findings.title: Token exchange and user info calls are not guarded against failures
findings.detail: `safe_urlopen` and `get_user_info` are called outside the try block. Network errors or a non-dict response from `get_user_info` raise an exception, and `"login" not in ...` may fail on a bad return, causing a 500 instead of the error page.

findings.title: Redirect URL query parameters are not URL-encoded
findings.detail: client_id, state and redirect_uri are interpolated into the authorize URL without urlencode, so special characters in redirect_uri (for example in a custom domain or port) can break or alter the query string.

findings.title: test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the 404 installation path
findings.detail: The test now passes a wrong state, so it fails with the generic 'Invalid installation request.' error from the state mismatch. The 404 branch in `build_integration` is never reached, and the first request's response is discarded.
findings.evidence: assert b"Invalid installation request." in resp.content

findings.title: Brittle assertion on the index of the recorded responses call
findings.detail: `responses.calls[2]` is used to find the JWT-authenticated request; this couples the test to the order and number of stubbed HTTP calls and does not verify the intended call.

findings.title: Existing-installation check skipped when Integration row is absent
findings.detail: When no Integration exists for the installation_id, the view calls pipeline.next_step() without verifying that the authenticated GitHub user owns or installed the app. The installation_id comes from the query string, so a user can pass any installation_id and the sender check never runs.

findings.title: KeyError when integration metadata lacks 'sender'
findings.detail: build_integration only stores metadata['sender'] when state has a sender. Existing integrations without it will raise KeyError (HTTP 500) at integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] instead of failing cleanly.

findings.title: OAuth state is only compared to a static pipeline signature
findings.detail: The state parameter is pipeline.signature, which is deterministic and not bound to the browser session or one-time nonce. It gives weak CSRF/login-CSRF protection. The state is also interpolated into the URL unencoded.

findings.title: Unguarded network calls in OAuth callback
findings.detail: safe_urlopen and get_user_info are called outside the try block. Network errors or non-JSON/error responses from get_user_info raise unhandled exceptions (500) rather than rendering the error page. A non-dict result would also break the `"login" not in` check.

findings.title: Redirect URL query parameters are not URL-encoded
findings.detail: The authorize redirect is built via an f-string with raw redirect_uri and state, so special characters are not escaped. The redirect_uri contains ':' and '/', which the test expects unencoded. This is fragile.

findings.title: test_installation_not_found no longer tests a 404 installation
findings.detail: The test now expects 'Invalid installation request.' caused by a mismatched state. It never reaches the 404 handling in build_integration, so the intended branch is untested. The 'could not be found' assertion was dropped.
findings.evidence: assert b"Invalid installation request." in resp.content

findings.title: Brittle index into responses.calls
findings.detail: The Authorization header is taken from a hardcoded responses.calls[2], which depends on how many OAuth calls precede it. It would not catch a wrong call ordering.

findings.title: KeyError when stored integration has no sender metadata
findings.detail: `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` is read directly, but `sender` is only set in metadata when the state contains it (see `build_integration`). Integrations created before this change, or without a sender, make the flow raise KeyError and return a 500 instead of a clean error.

findings.title: User-ownership check only runs for existing integrations
findings.detail: When no Integration exists, the code returns `pipeline.next_step()` without checking the authenticated GitHub user. The user check is therefore skipped on that path, and the identity is only verified when the Integration already exists.

findings.title: Token exchange and user lookup not guarded against network errors
findings.detail: `safe_urlopen` and `get_user_info` sit outside the try block, so network or HTTP errors raise an unhandled exception (500) instead of the friendly error page. Only the body-read step is wrapped, and it uses a broad `except Exception`.

findings.title: Redirect URL and state are not URL-encoded
findings.detail: The authorize URL is built by f-string interpolation without `urlencode`. `redirect_uri` is unescaped and the state is raw, which is fragile and can produce malformed or ambiguous query strings.

findings.title: test_installation_not_found no longer tests the 404 path
findings.detail: The test expects "Invalid installation request." and uses a different state value than the pipeline signature. It passes because of the state mismatch, not because the GitHub installation lookup returned 404, so the original behavior is no longer exercised.
findings.evidence: assert b"Invalid installation request." in resp.content

findings.title: Brittle index into responses.calls
findings.detail: The Authorization header is read from `responses.calls[2]`, a hardcoded index that depends on the order of the newly added OAuth stub calls. Reordering or adding calls would silently break or misattribute the assertion.

findings.title: Copied config with display schedule_type is built but not used
findings.detail: The code copies the config and swaps in the human-readable schedule_type, but the returned dict uses the original monitor.config. The copy is dead code and the display value never reaches the event context.

findings.title: Failure reason crashes or is wrong when no failed statuses are counted
findings.detail: If no check-in has an ERROR/MISSED/TIMEOUT status, status_counts is empty and the function returns " check-ins detected" with an empty list. A single failed check-in with a non-mapped status falls through to the same path. The docstring's "A failed check-in was detected" case is never implemented.

findings.title: Docstring examples do not match the output
findings.detail: The docstring promises "were detected" wording and an "A failed check-in was detected" message. The code always produces "... check-ins detected" and has no generic failed-check-in message. Also the count/status formatting yields "2 missed" rather than "2 missed check-ins".
findings.evidence: "2 missed check-ins, 1 timeout check-in and 1 error check-in were detected"

findings.title: Occurrence creation repeats per-check-in queries and sends the full list each time
findings.detail: For every failed check-in, create_incident_occurrence issues queries (get_last_successful_checkin, environment, monitor, owner_actor). With threshold N this means N occurrences, each doing redundant lookups. All occurrences use the same full previous_checkins list.

findings.title: Threshold check does not verify enough check-ins exist
findings.detail: If fewer than failure_issue_threshold check-ins exist and none are OK, the status is still moved to ERROR and an incident is created. The threshold is not actually enforced. The "commits" in the nearby comment is also a wrong word.

findings.title: Copied config with display schedule_type is built but never used
findings.detail: The code copies the config and swaps in the human-readable schedule_type, but the returned dict uses `monitor.config` instead of the modified `config`. The display conversion is dead code and the raw schedule_type goes into the event context.

findings.title: Failure reason crashes or is empty when no check-ins have a failure status
findings.detail: If no check-in has a status in HUMAN_FAILURE_STATUS_MAP, the count sum is 0, so the function falls through and yields " check-ins detected" with an empty list. The docstring's example outputs, such as "were detected" and "A failed check-in", do not match what the code actually produces.

findings.title: Threshold lookup slices queryset and may yield fewer check-ins than the threshold
findings.detail: When fewer than failure_issue_threshold check-ins exist, the code still treats the monitor as having hit the threshold, so an incident is created too early. In addition, previous_checkins[0] raises IndexError if the list is empty.

findings.title: Monitor status saved before incident creation without a transaction
findings.detail: The env status is set to ERROR and saved before get_or_create of the incident. If incident creation fails, the env stays in ERROR with no incident, and later failures take the ERROR branch where active_incident is None and no occurrence is produced.

findings.title: Occurrence emitted once per check-in using the whole list for each reason
findings.detail: For each check-in in the threshold window, an occurrence is created with the full previous_checkins list. Each one carries the same aggregated failure reason, and the queryset order of check-ins is unspecified.

findings.title: Computed config copy discarded; raw config sent in context
findings.detail: A copy of config is created and schedule_type is replaced with its display value, but the returned dict uses monitor.config instead of the modified copy. The humanized schedule_type is never applied and the copy is dead code.

findings.title: get_failure_reason crashes or yields empty text when no failed statuses
findings.detail: If no check-in has a status in HUMAN_FAILURE_STATUS_MAP (for example, a status like UNKNOWN or IN_PROGRESS), status_counts is empty, so the sum is 0. The code then produces the malformed string " check-ins detected". With exactly one counted status the singular path is used, but a mixed list still hides the other entries.

findings.title: Docstring examples do not match actual output
findings.detail: The docstring claims outputs like "were detected" and "A failed check-in was detected", but the code always produces "... check-ins detected" or "A <status> check-in was detected". It also contains typos ("humam readible").
findings.evidence: "2 missed check-ins, 1 timeout check-in and 1 error check-in were detected"

findings.title: Plural/singular wording wrong for per-status counts
findings.detail: The status text is the bare word (e.g. "2 missed"), then " check-ins detected" is appended, so mixed output reads "2 missed, 1 timeout and 1 error check-ins detected", contradicting the documented "2 missed check-ins, 1 timeout check-in" form.

findings.title: Status saved as ERROR before incident creation, not atomic
findings.detail: The monitor env status is saved to ERROR before the incident get_or_create, with no transaction. A failure in between, or a concurrent call, leaves the env in ERROR with no incident, so later failures find active_incident None and never create occurrences.

findings.title: Occurrence produced per check-in with repeated queries
findings.detail: For each of up to threshold check-ins, create_incident_occurrence is called, each time doing get_last_successful_checkin and related lookups. This runs N queries and produces N occurrences, and the filtered queryset has no ordering.

findings.title: Restart check skips sibling dead processes / restarts mutate dict during iteration
findings.detail: _create_process_for_shards assigns self.processes[process_index] while _ensure_processes_alive iterates self.processes.items(). Replacing a value for an existing key is allowed, but the restart logic is fragile. More importantly, restart counters are never reset, so long-lived consumers eventually crash after 10 restarts per process.

findings.title: join() breaks out of loop leaving remaining processes running
findings.detail: When the deadline expires the loop `break`s before terminating the remaining multiprocessing processes, so they are never terminated (and a timed-out process is only terminated if loop reached it). Also with timeout of 0/None the deadline handling is inconsistent.

findings.title: Shard-to-process mapping crashes when no shards are assigned
findings.detail: If buffer.assigned_shards is empty, num_processes is 0 and `i % self.num_processes` is never evaluated, but max_processes becomes 0 via `or`; with a non-empty list and max_processes=0 the same path is fine. However an empty assignment yields no flusher processes, so no flushing/health checks happen. Separately, `i % num_processes` raises ZeroDivisionError if max_processes is negative-clamped to 0.

findings.title: Inconsistent metric tag name 'shards' vs 'shard'
findings.detail: wait_produce timer uses the tag key 'shards' while the other metrics use 'shard', producing inconsistent dimensions for the same flusher metrics.

findings.title: Restarting a process creates a fresh SpansBuffer and leaks the old one
findings.detail: Every restart builds a new SpansBuffer (new Redis clients) and overwrites self.buffers entry; also the metric tag 'shard' on unhealthy incr produces per-shard high-cardinality tags.

findings.title: Dead code and docstring contradicting behavior
findings.detail: _create_process_for_shard is unused, and the docstring claims one process per shard while the code shares processes across shards based on max_processes.
findings.evidence: Creates one process per shard for parallel processing.

findings.title: Test patches time.sleep then relies on real sleep and is weak
findings.detail: time.sleep is monkeypatched to a no-op, so the added `time.sleep(0.1)` gives no wait and cannot synchronize with the flusher thread, making test_basic racy. The new test also never submits spans so it only checks the mapping.

findings.title: Restarted process buffer not used by the buffers dict consistently / stale buffers
findings.detail: Each restart builds a new SpansBuffer and overwrites self.buffers[process_index], and the old process is only killed after the new buffer is built. In threaded mode (produce_to_pipe) the old thread is never stopped, since only multiprocessing.Process gets kill(), so two threads can flush the same shards concurrently.

findings.title: isinstance check against multiprocessing.Process never matches SpawnProcess
findings.detail: The spawn context creates multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process (that is the default-context class). The isinstance check is therefore always False, so hung processes are never killed and join() never terminates them. Zombie flushers keep running against the same shards after restart.

findings.title: Shard-to-process mapping can divide by zero with no assigned shards
findings.detail: If buffer.assigned_shards is empty, num_processes becomes 0 (min(max_processes, 0)) and `i % self.num_processes` is never evaluated only because the loop is empty, but the flusher then has no processes and no buffers. Also with max_processes=0 passed explicitly, `or` falls back silently. Empty-shard consumers silently run no flushing.

findings.title: join() deadline handling skips terminating remaining processes
findings.detail: When the deadline expires, the loop breaks before terminating the remaining processes, leaving them running. Also a timeout of 0 gives deadline None, which waits forever.

findings.title: Backpressure and the shared drift/stopped values are coupled across processes
findings.detail: A single shared current_drift and stopped are used for all processes; backpressure from any one process rejects all messages, and the restart counter check `> MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS` is incremented before the check on each loop, so behavior differs per process. Also memory/flush metrics tagged with 'shards' vs 'shard' inconsistently.

findings.title: Test relies on real sleep after monkeypatching time.sleep to no-op
findings.detail: The test monkeypatches time.sleep to a no-op, so the added time.sleep(0.1) does nothing and the test is timing-dependent (flaky), not a real synchronization.

findings.title: Process limit test does not verify shard distribution
findings.detail: The test only checks the count of shards summed, not the round-robin assignment or that each process gets 2 shards, so wrong mappings would pass.
findings.evidence: assert total_shards == 4  # All 4 shards should be assigned

findings.title: Restarted process still tracked in old state; buffers dict stale / restart reuse
findings.detail: On restart, a new SpansBuffer is created and replaces self.buffers[process_index], while the killed process's shard state and `redis_was_full`/backpressure are kept. More importantly, `_create_process_for_shards` runs inside a loop iterating `self.processes.items()` and assigns `self.processes[process_index]`; this is OK for existing keys, but a hung process killed via `kill()` is only done for `multiprocessing.Process` while the spawn context returns `SpawnProcess`, which is not an instance of `multiprocessing.Process`.

findings.title: join never terminates SpawnProcess due to wrong isinstance check
findings.detail: mp_context.Process produces multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process (the class from process.py), so the isinstance check is always False. Flusher processes are never terminated in join() and hung ones are never killed on restart, leaving zombie/duplicate flushers on the same shards.

findings.title: join loop breaks without terminating remaining processes
findings.detail: When the deadline is exceeded, the loop `break`s, skipping terminate for all remaining processes. The shared timeout is also consumed by earlier processes.

findings.title: Stale buffer used for main process while flusher uses separate buffer; shared state split
findings.detail: The flusher creates new per-process SpansBuffer objects, but the consumer's `buffer` in the factory still covers all shards. Flushers' `any_shard_at_limit` is tracked per child buffer, and the buffers in the parent used for `record_stored_segments` / memory info are separate instances; memory is summed across per-process buffers which may query the same Redis multiple times, overcounting used/available and distorting the max-memory check.

findings.title: Zero shards causes modulo-by-zero
findings.detail: If buffer.assigned_shards is empty, max_processes becomes 0 (falsy `or` yields len==0), num_processes is 0 and `i % self.num_processes` is never reached only because the loop is empty, but any max_processes of 0/negative from CLI is silently replaced; negative values yield num_processes<=0 and a ZeroDivisionError or no flushers.

findings.title: Docstring claims one process per shard
findings.detail: The docstring says it creates one process per shard, but processes are capped by max_processes and shards are shared among them.
findings.evidence: Creates one process per shard for parallel processing.

findings.title: Test uses real time.sleep after monkeypatching it to no-op
findings.detail: time.sleep is monkeypatched to a no-op so the 'give flusher time' sleep does nothing, making the test timing-dependent/flaky. Also the new test never asserts flushing behavior with shared processes.

findings.title: Inconsistent metric tag names
findings.detail: One timer uses tag 'shard' while the adjacent wait_produce timer uses 'shards', splitting the metric dimension inconsistently.

findings.title: FromContext silently drops contextual attributes on type assertion failure
findings.detail: If the infra logger's FromContext does not return *log.ConcreteLogger, the code falls back to d.New(), which discards the request-scoped attributes. The "Plugin Request Completed" log would then lose pluginId, endpoint, dsName and the other attributes that were removed from logRequest.

findings.title: TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh logger, so assertions on logs are lost
findings.detail: FromContext returns a new TestLogger, so Info calls made through it are not recorded on the original TestLogger. Tests that inspect InfoLogs on the logger passed to LoggerMiddleware cannot see the "Plugin Request Completed" log.

findings.title: Stream endpoints do not get contextual logger attributes
findings.detail: SubscribeStream, PublishStream and RunStream pass the context through without adding plugin or request details, so logs for those calls lack the contextual attributes. The CallResource, QueryData, CheckHealth and CollectMetrics paths all add them, so the behaviour is inconsistent.

findings.title: traceID no longer included in the request log
findings.detail: The traceID was previously appended explicitly to the "Plugin Request Completed" log params, and the tracing import was removed. The new contextual logger middleware does not add a traceID attribute, so unless the logger's FromContext adds it, trace correlation is lost.

findings.title: FromContext drops contextual attributes on type assertion failure
findings.detail: If `d.l.FromContext(ctx)` does not return a `*log.ConcreteLogger`, the code falls back to `d.New()`, which discards all context-derived attributes (plugin id, endpoint, datasource, traceID). The request log then silently loses the fields the middleware change relies on.

findings.title: TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh logger, so logs are lost
findings.detail: FromContext returns a new TestLogger rather than the receiver, so anything logged through it is never recorded on the original logger. Tests of LoggerMiddleware that assert on `InfoLogs` will not see the 'Plugin Request Completed' call, since the middleware now logs via `FromContext`.

findings.title: Contextual logger middleware placed after metrics middleware
findings.detail: The old comment said the context-enriching middleware must be at the top of the stack. Now NewMetricsMiddleware runs before NewContextualLoggerMiddleware, so logs emitted by the metrics middleware lack the plugin/endpoint attributes. Any later change that logs there will miss them.

findings.title: traceID no longer explicitly added to request log
findings.detail: The explicit traceID log param was removed. It now depends on the contextual logger from the context carrying the trace ID, which `instrumentContext` does not add. The 'Plugin Request Completed' log may lose traceID, regressing existing behaviour.

findings.title: Nil request dereference in contextual logger middleware
findings.detail: `req.PluginContext` is dereferenced without a nil check, while LoggerMiddleware guards against nil requests. A nil request will panic here before reaching the guarded middleware.

findings.title: TestLogger.FromContext discards recorded logs
findings.detail: FromContext returns a brand new TestLogger, so the logger-middleware's Info call lands on a throwaway instance. Tests that inspect InfoLogs on the original logger can never observe the "Plugin Request Completed" call.

findings.title: FromContext type assertion silently drops contextual attributes
findings.detail: The result of d.l.FromContext(ctx) is asserted to *log.ConcreteLogger; if it is another Logger implementation, the fallback returns d.New(), losing the context attributes without any signal. Even on success, the logger's own name/context may differ from the wrapper's, so the fallback is a silent behavior change.

findings.title: traceID no longer included in request-completed log
findings.detail: The explicit traceID logging was removed and nothing in the contextual logger middleware adds a traceID attribute. If infra FromContext does not add the trace ID, the 'Plugin Request Completed' logs lose trace correlation.

findings.title: Contextual logger is not applied when no stream/plugin context is nil-checked
findings.detail: The new middleware dereferences req.PluginContext without a nil check on req, whereas LoggerMiddleware guards against nil req. A nil request will panic in the contextual middleware before reaching the guard downstream.

findings.title: Test name not updated and no test for new middleware
findings.detail: The test is still named TestInstrumentationMiddleware after the rename to MetricsMiddleware. No test was added for ContextualLoggerMiddleware or the FromContext-based logging, so moved behavior is untested.

findings.title: Denial cache hides newly granted permissions for the full TTL
findings.detail: A negative result is cached for 30s and consulted before the DB fallback. Permissions granted after a denial (or changed role/team membership) are still denied until the entry expires, which defeats the 'fallback to DB on outdated cache' design.

findings.title: Denial cache key can collide with the permission cache key
findings.detail: The key reuses the ".perm_<uid>_<action>" prefix of userPermCacheKey and just appends name/parent, with no separator or distinct prefix. It can collide with other keys, e.g. an action containing underscores or empty name/parent, and with anonymous keys. Name/parent concatenation with '_' is also ambiguous between different (name,parent) pairs.
findings.evidence: return namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent

findings.title: Cached-permission error during Check aborts instead of falling back to DB
findings.detail: If getCachedIdentityPermissions fails (e.g. identifier lookup), the error is silently swallowed and the code falls through, but a checkPermission error on cached perms returns immediately. Also, checkPermission against stale cached perms may trigger a folder-tree build with its own failure that denies without trying the DB path.

findings.title: Cache usage metric is miscounted and denial lookup bypasses user-id resolution
findings.detail: The 'false' cache-usage metric is incremented even when the cache lookup failed with a real error or when cached perms exist but were insufficient, and the denial cache is checked with the raw request UserUID (not the resolved UID used elsewhere), so a numeric ID and a UID for the same user use different keys.

findings.title: Permission cache check removed from getUserPermissions and getAnonymousPermissions
findings.detail: These functions no longer consult permCache, so any caller of getIdentityPermissions always hits the DB (guarded only by singleflight). The cache check now exists only in the separate Check/List paths, and the corresponding test case was deleted rather than adapted.

findings.title: In-proc client now uses a no-op cache
findings.detail: The in-process client previously used a 30s local cache; the NoopCache disables client-side caching entirely, making every check go through the RBAC service. This also silently changes the behaviour for the shadow-client path.

findings.title: Deny-cache test uses an unrealistic stale permCache value and doesn't check store calls
findings.detail: The test comment says it proves the permCache isn't checked, but permCache has the scope set to false which would deny anyway (scopeMap[...] false), so it cannot distinguish the denial-cache short-circuit from normal flow.

findings.title: Denial cache key collides with permission cache key and ignores action-set semantics
findings.detail: userPermDenialCacheKey is namespace.perm_<uid>_<action>_<name>_<parent>, sharing the `.perm_` prefix with userPermCacheKey. A user UID or action containing underscores can produce a key equal to another entry in the same shared cache, and fields are joined with `_` without escaping, so different (name,parent) tuples can collide. A stale denial lasts 30s even after permissions are granted, and a collision can cause incorrect denies.

findings.title: Denial cache keyed by raw UserUID but identity type is ignored
findings.detail: The denial key uses checkReq.UserUID without identity type. An anonymous:0, render:0 or user:0 subject (all UID '0') share the same key for the same action/name/folder, so a denial for one identity type (e.g. anonymous) is returned for another (e.g. a user with numeric id 0, or renderer), producing wrong denies.

findings.title: Cache-miss path counted as a cache hit for denied/absent and metrics mislabeled
findings.detail: permissionCacheUsage 'false' is incremented whenever the cached permissions did not allow, including when the cache was populated but outdated, and also when getCachedIdentityPermissions errored. Also the user-identity lookup in getCachedIdentityPermissions may hit the DB (GetUserIdentifiers) and its error is silently swallowed, then repeated by the fallback path.

findings.title: Denial cached for results derived from possibly-stale/failed folder data
findings.detail: Denials are cached for every non-allowed result, including requests where the folder tree was cached/stale or the permission was just granted; the denial entry is never invalidated, so newly granted access remains denied for up to 30 seconds even though the fresh DB permissions were just consulted.

findings.title: Removed cache-hit test and cacheHit branch is now dead in getUserPermissions test
findings.detail: The cache-hit case for getUserPermissions was deleted, leaving a cacheHit field and branches that are never exercised; also the 'should return error if store fails' case does not set err and does not expect an error, so it cannot catch error handling.
findings.evidence: name: "should return error if store fails",

findings.title: Deny test uses cache value false and claims it proves permCache is unused
findings.detail: The permCache entry is set to false for dash1, which would also result in deny, so the comment 'Allow access to prove this is not checked' is wrong and the test cannot distinguish that the denial cache short-circuited the check.

findings.title: newRemoteRBACClient error dropped by caller in cloud mode
findings.detail: In ProvideAuthZClient the error from newRemoteRBACClient is checked only after the Zanzana branch, so a nil client may be passed to WithShadowClient when creation failed.

findings.title: Negative-decision cache is never invalidated and bypasses fresh permissions
findings.detail: A denial is cached per user/action/name/folder, and while the entry lives every later Check returns deny without consulting permissions. A permission granted within the TTL window stays denied, and the cached-allow path also trusts stale grants.

findings.title: Denial cache key can collide with permission cache key and among fields
findings.detail: The key shares the prefix `namespace.perm_user_action` with userPermCacheKey, and fields are joined with underscores without escaping. Names or folders containing underscores can make different (name, parent) pairs map to the same key, so a denial for one resource can wrongly deny another.
findings.evidence: return namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent

findings.title: Cache usage metrics recorded inconsistently / double counted
findings.detail: The denial-cache hit is counted as a permission cache hit. When the cached permissions do not allow, the miss is recorded even though the cache existed. The `permissionCacheUsage` metric no longer reflects real permCache hit rates, and the checkPermission error path increments requestCount without a cache metric.

findings.title: Duplicate permission evaluation on cache-deny path
findings.detail: When cached permissions don't allow, Check falls through to getIdentityPermissions and then checkPermission again. Each denied request does two evaluations, including a possible folder tree build, and hits the DB every time the cache says deny before the denial entry is set.
findings.evidence: permissions, err := s.getIdentityPermissions(ctx, checkReq.Namespace, checkReq.IdentityType, checkReq.UserUID, checkReq.Action)

findings.title: Error from cached-permission lookup is silently swallowed
findings.detail: If getCachedIdentityPermissions fails (e.g. a user identifier lookup error), err is ignored and execution falls through to the DB path. The error is neither logged nor counted, and the failing lookup is repeated.
findings.evidence: cachedPerms, err := s.getCachedIdentityPermissions(ctx, checkReq.Namespace, checkReq.IdentityType, checkReq.UserUID, checkReq.Action)

findings.title: Cached lookup uses different key for anonymous/user than fallback path with action sets
findings.detail: The cache read ignores that folders:create permission queries are built with extra actionSets, while the key depends only on action. The code relies on the same key, which is fine, but a renderer returns ErrNotFound, so an unsupported renderer is metered as a cache miss on every call.

findings.title: getUserPermissions test keeps cacheHit logic but case removed
findings.detail: The cacheHit branches in the test are now dead because getUserPermissions no longer reads the cache, and no test covers permDenialCache being populated after a denial, or the cached-permission path for anonymous users.

findings.title: Device limit check-then-insert is racy and exceeds limit
findings.detail: CreateOrUpdateDevice counts devices and then inserts in separate, non-transactional statements. Concurrent requests can all see count < limit and all insert, exceeding the configured limit.

findings.title: Local cache set before store write; failure poisons cache
findings.detail: tagDeviceUI marks the device as cached before CreateOrUpdateDevice runs. When ErrDeviceLimitReached (or any DB error) is returned, the cache entry remains, so subsequent requests from that device skip tagging and are allowed through anonymously for the cache lifetime, bypassing the limit. The rejection is therefore not consistently enforced.

findings.title: Device tagging moved from async goroutine to synchronous auth path
findings.detail: TagDevice, with DB count and write queries, now runs inline on every anonymous request's authentication. This adds latency and DB load to the request path, and the removed 2-minute timeout and panic recovery are gone.

findings.title: Device-limit check is racy (count then insert)
findings.detail: The COUNT and subsequent INSERT are not atomic, so concurrent requests from new devices can all observe count < limit and all insert, exceeding the configured limit.

findings.title: updateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached for any zero-row update

findings.title: Exclusive lock taken without re-checking cache (no double-checked locking)
findings.detail: After the read lock is released, every caller that saw a nil cache takes the write lock and reloads the manifest. Concurrent requests at startup each redo the file read, and in Dev mode every request serializes behind the exclusive lock. The cache is not re-checked after acquiring the write lock.

findings.title: Failed load overwrites valid cache with nil
findings.detail: entryPointAssetsCache is assigned unconditionally, even when err != nil and result is nil. In Dev mode a transient read or parse error wipes the previously cached assets. The error is also returned alongside a nil value, so callers may dereference nil.

findings.title: CDN error is overwritten and result may be nil on file failure
findings.detail: If the CDN path is taken and fails, the error is silently overwritten by the file read. If the file read fails, result is nil and err is set. On success `cdn, _ =` ignores the error from GetContentDeliveryURL.

findings.title: Exclusive lock taken without re-checking cache (no double-checked locking)
findings.detail: After the read lock is released, every concurrent caller that saw a nil cache takes the write lock and re-reads the manifest, serializing redundant file/CDN loads. The cache is not re-checked under the write lock, so the first-load work is repeated N times. In Dev mode, every request also takes the exclusive lock and blocks the others during file I/O.

findings.title: Failed load overwrites a valid cached value with nil
findings.detail: The cache is assigned unconditionally, even when reading failed (result nil, err non-nil). In Dev mode a transient read error wipes a previously good cached value. The function returns a nil result along with the error, which callers may dereference.

findings.title: Exclusive lock taken without re-checking the cache (thundering herd)
findings.detail: After the RLock check misses, every concurrent caller serializes on the write Lock and each re-reads the manifest file, because the cache is not re-checked once the lock is held. Only the first caller needs to load it, so cold-start requests do redundant file I/O under an exclusive lock.

findings.title: In Dev mode every call takes the exclusive lock and re-reads the file
findings.detail: When cfg.Env is Dev the cache is bypassed and each call holds the global write lock while doing file I/O. All concurrent requests are serialized, and the RLock read is wasted work.

findings.title: Cache overwritten with nil result on error
findings.detail: entryPointAssetsCache is assigned unconditionally even when loading failed and result is nil. A transient failure erases a previously good cached value; because it's updated under the lock, other callers then see nil and reload.

findings.title: Error from CDN read is overwritten / nil result dereference risk
findings.detail: If the CDN read fails, err is overwritten by the file read path. Additionally, if result is nil from the file path with err==nil is not guarded, though SetContentDeliveryURL is only called on success, so the CDN error is silently lost.

The non-inline branch also relies on the batch size staying under the limit, rather than on len(ids).

Building the string with repeated Sprintf is also O(n^2).

findings.detail: The helper always returns false, so every SQL query is rejected with 'sqlExpressions is not implemented' regardless of the feature toggle state. The message does not say whether the feature is disabled or not implemented.
findings.evidence: return eq, fmt.Errorf("sqlExpressions is not implemented")

findings.title: Stub DB methods return 'not implemented' for all calls
findings.detail: RunCommands and QueryFramesInto unconditionally fail, so sql.TablesList always returns an error and NewSQLCommand always fails with 'error reading SQL command'. The existing SQL expression path is broken for any caller that doesn't pass through the reader gate (e.g. UnmarshalSQLCommand).

findings.title: Unused stub method TablesList on DB duplicates package function
findings.detail: DB.TablesList is a dead stub that shadows the semantic of package-level TablesList and always returns an error, which is misleading.

findings.title: Execute failures swallowed into result with nil error
findings.detail: Query errors from the now-stub DB are put into rsp.Error while returning nil error; combined with the stub this makes every execution silently yield an error result. Also NoData result is overwritten afterwards when Rows()==0.

findings.title: enableSqlExpressions always returns false regardless of feature flag
findings.detail: Both branches return false: if the flag is enabled, `enabled` is false and it returns false; otherwise it also returns false. The flag value is also inverted in the intermediate variable. SQL expressions can never be enabled through the reader even when the feature toggle is on.

findings.title: Misleading error when SQL expressions are disabled or unavailable
findings.detail: The error 'sqlExpressions is not implemented' is returned even when the feature toggle is enabled, because the helper always returns false. It also misreports a disabled feature as unimplemented.
findings.evidence: return eq, fmt.Errorf("sqlExpressions is not implemented")

findings.title: Stub DB methods always fail, breaking sql.TablesList and SQLCommand paths
findings.detail: RunCommands and QueryFramesInto unconditionally return 'not implemented', so TablesList and NewSQLCommand always fail with an error. The other call sites (UnmarshalSQLCommand, the expression pipeline) have no guard for this, so any path that reaches them fails.

findings.title: Unused/dead TablesList method on DB duplicates package-level function
findings.detail: DB.TablesList is a stub that ignores its input and shadows the semantics of the package-level TablesList in parser.go; it is never used and returns an error.

findings.title: go.sum hash entries moved to go.work.sum while other checksums removed
findings.detail: Several go.sum h1 hashes (e.g. gotest.tools/v3 v3.5.1, araddon/dateparse) were removed from go.sum while still possibly required by workspace modules; the go.work.sum now carries partial entries, which risks missing-checksum errors.

findings.title: enableSqlExpressions always returns false regardless of the feature flag
findings.detail: Both branches return false: when the flag is on, `enabled` is false so the function falls through to `return false`, and when the flag is off it returns false as well. SQL expressions can never be enabled through this reader, even when FlagSqlExpressions is set.

findings.title: Inverted flag variable named 'enabled'
findings.detail: `enabled` is assigned the negation of the feature flag, so it actually means 'disabled'. Combined with the unconditional false return, the logic contradicts its names and is hard to fix correctly.

findings.title: Misleading error message when the feature is merely disabled
findings.detail: The error says 'sqlExpressions is not implemented' even though the check is meant to gate on a feature toggle. Users with the flag enabled will still be told the feature is not implemented, and a disabled flag is not reported as such.
findings.evidence: return eq, fmt.Errorf("sqlExpressions is not implemented")

findings.title: Stub DB makes SQL expression path always fail
findings.detail: RunCommands and QueryFramesInto always return 'not implemented'. As a result, TablesList and SQLCommand.Execute fail for every query, so the SQL expression feature is broken outside of the reader gate. NewSQLCommand is also reachable via UnmarshalSQLCommand, which has no gate.

findings.title: Unused DB.TablesList stub
findings.detail: The DB.TablesList method duplicates the package-level TablesList function but is a dead stub that always returns an error, so it is misleading.

findings.title: Targets interpolated twice in the sharding path (ad-hoc filters applied twice)
findings.detail: runShardSplitQuery interpolates targets with applyTemplateVariables. Each shard sub-request then goes through runSplitQuery, which interpolates again using the same request.filters. Ad-hoc filters can be injected twice, and interpolated values containing '$' can be re-expanded.

findings.title: Interpolation before runQuery repeats work the query path already does
findings.detail: runSplitQuery now interpolates every target, and each sub-request is then sent to datasource.runQuery, which interpolates again through the backend query path. This applies ad-hoc filters and variable replacement twice, which can duplicate filters or re-expand values.

findings.title: Test asserts the double-interpolation call count
findings.detail: The test expects applyTemplateVariables to be called 5 times: once in runShardSplitQuery plus once per sub-request. This locks in the redundant repeated interpolation and breaks on any change to the number of shard groups. It does not check that interpolation is correct.

findings.title: Queries interpolated twice in shard path (including ad-hoc filters)
findings.detail: runShardSplitQuery applies applyTemplateVariables with request.filters, then each shard sub-request goes through runSplitQuery, which applies it again to the already-interpolated queries. Ad-hoc filters can be injected twice, and already-substituted values containing `$` can be re-interpolated.

findings.title: Interpolating before the split check changes isQueryWithRangeVariable behaviour
findings.detail: querySupportsSplitting checks `$__range` in the expr, but targets are now interpolated first, so the variable may already be replaced and the query gets split. The comment on querySupportsSplitting is now out of date, and the backend then interpolates the query a second time.

findings.title: Test hardcodes the double-interpolation call count
findings.detail: Expecting applyTemplateVariables to be called 5 times (1 in runShardSplitQuery plus 4 in runSplitQuery) locks in redundant interpolation. It also no longer verifies that interpolation happens once before running.

findings.title: Mock mutates its input query, hiding double-interpolation and mutation problems
findings.detail: The applyTemplateVariables mock mutates and returns the same query object. The real implementation returns a new object, so the tests can pass even if the code mishandles request.targets when interpolating.

findings.title: Queries are interpolated twice on the shard splitting path
findings.detail: runShardSplitQuery interpolates every target, then each shard sub-request goes through runSplitQuery, which now interpolates again. Re-running applyTemplateVariables on already-interpolated queries can re-apply ad-hoc filters (duplicating them in the expr), re-escape values, or expand `$` text that appeared in a substituted value. It also repeats the work for every shard group.

findings.title: Test asserts the redundant repeated interpolation as expected behaviour
findings.detail: The assertion expects applyTemplateVariables to run 5 times for a single query, which is 1 call from the shard entry point plus 4 from the nested runSplitQuery calls. This hard-codes the double interpolation, so the test will not flag it as a problem and will break if the duplication is removed.

findings.title: Empty-expression filter runs before interpolation
findings.detail: The `query.expr` filter runs before applyTemplateVariables. A query whose expression is only a variable that resolves to an empty string passes the filter and is sent on with an empty expr. This is inconsistent with the intent of dropping empty queries.

findings.title: Rolling-updates feature not enabled when updateStrategy is null
findings.detail: createInitialDeployment returns early when updateStrategy is null, so the ROLLING_UPDATES feature is never enabled for the null-strategy cases. Those cases (including the rolling upgrade status checks) depend on the feature, so they run without it and the Operator fails or does not behave as the test expects.

findings.title: Exit code for recreate upgrade changed from 4 to 3
findings.detail: The RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE was changed from 4 to 3 and 4 now means feature disabled. Existing scripts or operator code that rely on exit code 4 to mean recreate will now misinterpret a disabled feature as a recreate upgrade, and a real recreate (3) will not be recognized.

findings.title: Doc template appends --features after all parameters
findings.detail: The macro always appends --features=rolling-updates to every update-compatibility example, so the displayed command always carries the preview flag. This is misleading for docs and may break if parameters already include a --features option.

findings.title: Feature-disabled test does not verify the exit code
findings.detail: testFeatureNotEnabled only asserts the error message and does not check the new exit code (4). It also launches only the metadata subcommand, so the check command's disabled path is not covered.
findings.evidence: cliResult.assertError("Unable to use this command. The preview feature 'rolling-updates' is not enabled.");

findings.title: Feature enablement is skipped when updateStrategy is null
findings.detail: createInitialDeployment returns early when updateStrategy is null, so the rolling-updates feature is only enabled for the RECREATE case. The null-strategy cases (testImageChange-null, testCacheMaxCount-null) expect rolling upgrade behaviour and will fail or behave differently because the feature is disabled.

findings.title: Feature flag appended after all parameters
findings.detail: The macro unconditionally appends `--features=rolling-updates` to every update-compatibility example, so users copy a command that would pass the option twice if they also add `--features`. It also puts the option after the file parameter, which makes the docs sample misleading and non-composable.

findings.title: Exit code for recreate upgrade changed, breaking existing consumers
findings.detail: RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE changes from 4 to 3, so scripts that rely on the previous contract will misinterpret the result. Other code or docs referencing code 4 as recreate can also become inconsistent, and code 4 now means feature disabled.

findings.title: Feature check runs before config validation and may NPE if profile not configured
findings.detail: Profile.isFeatureEnabled dereferences Profile.getInstance(), which is null if the profile has not been initialised. In addition, the feature-disabled path returns before validateConfig, so option errors are hidden behind the feature message.

findings.title: Docs say feature-disabled exit code but the command prints a message with picocli.exit
findings.detail: The documentation says 'Otherwise, the commands will fail' while the exit code table lists a 'Rolling Upgrade is not possible' meaning for 4. The exit code actually means the command was refused rather than a recreate upgrade being required, which is misleading for scripts that treat non-zero as recreate.

findings.title: Rolling-updates feature enabled only when a strategy is set
findings.detail: createInitialDeployment returns early when updateStrategy is null, so the feature is never enabled for the default case. The null-strategy variants run without the preview feature, and the test only passes if the operator tolerates a disabled feature.

findings.title: Feature check happens after config may be needed / exit code ambiguous
findings.detail: The feature check runs before validateConfig. If a persisted build already has the feature disabled, the command returns FEATURE_DISABLED (4), which was previously the recreate-upgrade code. Scripts that treat 4 as 'recreate upgrade' now misinterpret the result, and the exit codes changed without any compatibility note.

findings.title: Doc table lists feature-disabled as 'Rolling Upgrade is not possible'
findings.detail: Exit code 4 means the command did not run because the feature is disabled; it is not an upgrade-compatibility verdict. Describing it as 'Rolling Upgrade is not possible' misleads automation that treats non-zero codes as 'recreate'. The doc also does not mention that the recreate code changed from 4 to 3.

findings.title: Macro appends --features after all parameters unconditionally
findings.detail: The macro puts `--features=rolling-updates` at the end of every example. This is hidden from the doc text and shows the flag in examples where it is not necessarily explained. Appending it after `${parameters}` also breaks the case where parameters end with a positional or end-of-options marker.

findings.title: Login cache not invalidated when organization link or other IDP changes affect it
findings.detail: The cached login lists are keyed per FetchMode, but each one stores a different searchKey inside a single query. A cache hit for `ORG_ONLY` with a null organizationId and one with a specific orgId share the same key and are told apart only by searchKey, and a lookup miss calls `invalidateObject` and rebuilds. The IDs are resolved with `session.identityProviders().getById`, so a stale entry also forces fallback. Worse, `registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate` compares `original` and `updated` using `getLoginPredicate`. That predicate is evaluated on a model whose organizationId may not be set yet at update time, because the org link is made via a separate update path. Cache invalidation can therefore be skipped for org membership changes.

findings.title: remove() may pass null IDP to invalidation and NPE
findings.detail: `storedIdp` is fetched from the delegate before the removal and can be null if the alias does not exist. In the `isInvalid` branch `registerIDPInvalidation(storedIdp)` dereferences it. `registerIDPLoginInvalidation` handles null through `Objects::nonNull`, but the other branch does not. Removing a nonexistent alias should return false, not throw an NPE.

findings.title: getConfig() may be null in login predicate
findings.detail: The new predicate dereferences `idp.getConfig().get(...)` for IDPs with an organization. If config is null, this throws an NPE inside stream or invalidation logic. The predicate is also redundant with the `BROKER_PUBLIC` search option already added by `getForLogin`.

findings.title: Cached login IDs returned from getById lose enabled-check ordering and ignore org state
findings.detail: The cached login list is built from IDs of IDPs that were enabled at cache time. An organization being disabled or removed does not invalidate the `.idp.login` caches, so the cache retains IDPs of disabled orgs. This is why callers must re-check `isEnabled`. Other consumers of `getForLogin` do not re-check, so they can return IDPs that should not be offered.

findings.title: Cleanup registered with literal alias "alias" instead of created IDP
findings.detail: The cleanup lambda removes the IDP with alias "alias", which does not exist, so the created IDPs are never cleaned up. This leaks IDPs into later tests and can break their expectations.

findings.title: remove() can NPE when the alias does not exist
findings.detail: storedIdp is fetched from the delegate and may be null for an unknown alias. It is passed to registerIDPInvalidation, which dereferences it, in the isInvalid branch. The remove(alias) contract is to return false for a missing IDP, so this changes it to an exception. The cached branch can also hit it via getLoginPredicate when the IDP is only cached.

findings.title: Login cache key ignores organizationId, so one org's results are served to another
findings.detail: The cache key depends only on realm and FetchMode, while the organizationId is only the searchKey inside the query. Invalidation drops the whole entry when a new searchKey arrives (invalidateObject followed by a new query built from the old one), so it thrashes between organizations. The cache also stores results for one org and serves them correctly only if the query's per-searchKey sets stay consistent.

findings.title: Login cache not invalidated when an org is enabled/disabled or IDP is wrapped; cached login IDPs may be stale
findings.detail: Cached IDs are re-resolved with getById, but the idp may be enabled/disabled via organization state. The result is not re-filtered against the login predicate, so a stale entry can be returned. This is why the callers had to add isEnabled re-checks, but the organization-aware path in OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean for organization.getIdentityProviders is not covered.

findings.title: Update invalidation ignores changes to organization link when the IDP is not a login IDP
findings.detail: The login predicate was changed to require a public flag for org-linked IDPs, but update() compares only the old and new model state. If getById returns a wrapped model, original.isEnabled() depends on the organization state, so the comparison can be inconsistent with what the delegate's getForLogin returned. A stale cache can then result.

findings.title: getConfig() may be null in the new login predicate
findings.detail: The added predicate dereferences idp.getConfig() without a null check. A model with a null config and an organization id will throw an NPE when the predicate is evaluated during cache invalidation.

findings.title: Cleanup registered for wrong alias
findings.detail: The cleanup removes the IDP with the literal alias "alias" instead of the one created, so the created IDPs are never cleaned up. This leaks state into other tests.

findings.title: Test calls getForLogin without consuming the stream
findings.detail: The result of getForLogin is discarded and never consumed. The assertions rely on the cache being populated eagerly, which works only because the implementation collects into a Set. The test would not catch a lazy implementation.

findings.title: Login cache keyed only by mode, but results depend on organizationId
findings.detail: The cache key is realm+mode, and the per-organization results are held as separate searchKeys in one query object. Invalidation of an IDP that belongs to a different org still works, but the stored organizationId searchKey for non-REALM_ONLY modes is only reconstructed through repeated invalidateObject calls. Every new organizationId evicts the entry and replaces it, causing cache thrash and possible stale data across concurrent requests.

findings.title: Login invalidation misses IDPs whose login eligibility changes via org membership or deletion of org
findings.detail: In registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate the update model may not yet carry the new organization link (it is set separately via addIdentityProvider/IDP link). Also org-level changes (org disabled/removed, IDP unlinked) do not invalidate the login cache, so cached login lists go stale and can include IDPs that no longer qualify.

findings.title: remove() may pass null IDP to registerIDPInvalidation
findings.detail: storedIdp is looked up from the delegate before the removal. If the alias does not exist it is null, and registerIDPInvalidation(storedIdp) dereferences it, throwing an NPE instead of returning false. The previous code had the same lookup but only on that branch; now it is evaluated unconditionally, though the NPE risk remains in the invalid branch.

findings.title: Cached login results do not account for organization enabled state
findings.detail: IDPs bound to a disabled organization are excluded only via the wrapper's isEnabled, but getForLogin on cache hit returns models via getById, and the cached set was computed from the delegate. Toggling an organization's enabled state does not invalidate the login cache and the cached set is not re-filtered.

findings.title: getConfig().get may NPE and predicate changes semantics of login filter
findings.detail: The added predicate dereferences idp.getConfig() without null check. It also changes the shared login predicate so org-linked IDPs without BROKER_PUBLIC are excluded, affecting every caller of getLoginPredicate.

findings.title: Cleanup registered for wrong alias
findings.detail: Cleanup removes the IDP with the literal alias "alias" rather than the created alias, so the created IDPs are never cleaned up and can leak into other tests.

findings.title: TotalDocs() called without cache lock while the watch goroutine can write the map
findings.detail: The new log line calls s.search.TotalDocs(), which iterates bleveBackend.cache without taking cacheMu. The event-handling goroutine started just above can call BuildIndex and write to that map at the same time, causing a concurrent map read/write panic or a data race.

findings.title: BuildIndex no longer serialized; concurrent builds of the same key are possible
findings.detail: The lock that covered the whole build was removed and now guards only the map write. Init workers and getOrCreateIndex (GetIndex then build) can build the same namespaced resource concurrently. For file-backed indexes the second bleve.New on the same dir fails, and for in-memory indexes the last writer silently replaces the cached index.

findings.title: Stop() state is no longer enforced after per-request Init checks were removed
findings.detail: Init is now called once in the constructor, and the per-request s.Init(ctx) calls were removed. Stop() still sets s.initErr to 'service is stopping' or 'stopped', but no handler reads it any more. Requests are therefore served after shutdown. Init failures also now surface only at construction.

findings.title: Integration test disabled for postgres instead of fixed
findings.detail: The only test that exercises the storage-server target now skips entirely on postgres. This hides the failure that the eager Init change may be causing, and leaves that path with no CI coverage.
findings.evidence: t.Skip("skipping - test not working with postgres in Drone. Works locally.")

findings.title: TotalDocs() called while event goroutine may mutate the index cache
findings.detail: The new log line calls s.search.TotalDocs() after the handleEvent goroutine has started. The bleve TotalDocs iterates b.cache without taking cacheMu, while BuildIndex (called from handleEvent via getOrCreateIndex) writes to the same map. This can cause a concurrent map read/write panic.

findings.title: BuildIndex no longer serialized; concurrent builds of the same key race
findings.detail: The function-wide lock was removed and the mutex now guards only the cache write. Two concurrent builds for the same key (init workers plus getOrCreateIndex from Search or handleEvent) both run the builder. For file-backed indexes bleve.New on the same directory fails, and for in-memory indexes one build silently overwrites the other and leaks the first index.

findings.title: Init moved into constructor; request paths no longer honour init/stop state
findings.detail: Init errors are now only checked at construction. Stop() still sets s.initErr to 'service is stopping/stopped', but no handler (Create, Update, Read, List, Watch and so on) checks it any more, so requests are still served after shutdown. The constructor also blocks on a full index build, and on failure it returns without calling the context's cancel func, leaking the context.

findings.title: Integration test disabled for postgres
findings.detail: The test is skipped entirely for postgres rather than fixed. This removes coverage of the changed server initialization against a real DB and may hide a regression introduced by eager Init.
findings.evidence: t.Skip("skipping - test not working with postgres in Drone. Works locally.")

findings.title: BuildIndex no longer serialized; concurrent builds of the same key race
findings.detail: The function-wide lock was removed and only the cache write is locked. getOrCreateIndex has no per-key guard, so concurrent searches or watch events for the same missing index can each build it. For file-backed indexes the second bleve.New on the same directory fails, and for memory indexes one index is overwritten and leaked.

findings.title: TotalDocs called while the index cache is being mutated, without locking
findings.detail: bleveBackend.TotalDocs iterates b.cache without taking cacheMu. BuildIndex now writes the cache under its own lock, and the event goroutine started just above can call BuildIndex concurrently. This is a concurrent map read and write that can panic or race.

findings.title: Stop() state is no longer enforced because per-request Init checks were removed
findings.detail: Init now runs once in the constructor, and Stop sets s.initErr to "service is stopping" or "service is stopped". No request handler checks s.initErr any more, so a stopped server keeps serving Create, Update, Read and the other calls instead of rejecting them.

findings.title: Context cancel function leaked when eager Init fails
findings.detail: When Init fails, NewResourceServer returns nil, err without calling cancel. The cancelable context, and any watcher goroutines already started by a partially completed Init, stay alive. The error is also logged twice, here and inside Init.

findings.title: ECDSA test uses the default EC curve for every algorithm
findings.detail: KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair() uses the JDK default curve (typically P-256) for ES256, ES384 and ES512. The ES384 and ES512 signatures are therefore not P-384/P-521 sized, so the test does not exercise the signature lengths it claims to cover and may fail or pass for the wrong reason. A fixed round trip also only checks self-consistency, so it can mask encoding errors.

findings.title: Sequence parsing can loop forever or mis-count with indefinite length
findings.detail: readLength returns -1 for indefinite length, so the `length > 0` loop is skipped and an empty list is returned silently. The loop also subtracts only the element length, not the header bytes consumed by readNext, so a malformed element can mis-count. Combined with `length >= limit` in readLength, the parser is fragile on malformed input.

findings.title: Length check rejects valid inputs and read(length) can be negative or oversized
findings.detail: readInteger and readNext call read(length) with a length that may be -1 (indefinite). That produces a NegativeArraySizeException instead of an IOException. The `length >= limit` check applies only to the long form, so short-form lengths larger than the remaining data are only caught later.

findings.title: High tag number parsing: -1 passes validation and tag bits are not reset on EOF
findings.detail: If read() returns -1 after the 0x1f marker, `(b & 0x7f)` is 0x7f so the check passes, as the comment admits. The code relies on a later EOF check, and tagNo shifting can overflow for long tag sequences with no bounds check.

findings.title: Redundant encoder calls and mismatched integer sizing in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
findings.detail: Two ASN1Encoder.create().write(...) calls produce results that are discarded. The r/s arrays are padded with a leading zero byte, which forces a positive BigInteger but also yields non-minimal encoding handling that depends on BigInteger normalization.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns a non-BouncyCastle provider
findings.detail: The method name and contract promise a BouncyCastle security provider, but it returns the default KeyStore's provider (SUN). BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER derives from this value, so any code that looks up BC services by that name may fail.

findings.title: Log message passed as format string and tie order not deterministic
findings.detail: The builder string is passed directly as the format argument of debugf, so class names containing '%' would be misinterpreted. A trailing ", " is left in the message. Providers with equal order are chosen by service-loading order, with no error for ambiguity, silently removing the old multiple-provider safety check.

findings.title: getKeyStore uses enum name() rather than toString()
findings.detail: Other providers use format.toString() as the KeyStore type, while this one uses format.name(). If KeystoreFormat.toString() differs from the enum name (e.g. for PKCS12 or BCFKS), the wrong type is requested.

findings.title: Test uses default EC key size for every algorithm
findings.detail: The key pair is generated with the default EC size (256 bits on typical JDKs) and reused for ES256, ES384 and ES512. Signatures are therefore always P-256 sized, while the signLength passed is 64, 96 or 132, so the 384 and 512 cases exercise padding rather than real signature lengths. The round-trip passes trivially and would not catch size-specific bugs.

findings.title: readSequence loop breaks on indefinite length and long-form headers
findings.detail: readLength returns -1 for indefinite encoding, so the while loop is skipped and an empty list is returned silently. The loop also subtracts only each element's length from the remaining length, which is only valid when the length bytes count is already included. readNext's returned array includes header bytes, which happens to match, but there is no check for negative or overflowing remaining length, so truncated or garbage content is not detected.

findings.title: Non-checked ArrayIndexOutOfBounds and NegativeArraySize in read(int)
findings.detail: read(length) allocates new byte[length] with no guard against a negative length. An indefinite-length integer (-1) throws NegativeArraySizeException instead of IOException. Malformed signatures cause unchecked exceptions.

findings.title: Redundant discarded encoder calls and leading zero padding
findings.detail: Two ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to but discarded, which is dead code. Also, r and s are copied at offset 1 into a len+1 array, so they are always interpreted as positive; the logic is correct but the dead calls are wasteful.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns a non-BouncyCastle provider
findings.detail: The method returns the provider of the default KeyStore type (e.g. SUN) although the contract says it returns a BouncyCastle provider. Callers that depend on the BC provider name or class will get the wrong provider.

findings.title: Log message passed as format string
findings.detail: The built string, containing class names, is passed as the format argument to debugf. If it contains '%' characters, formatting will misbehave. The string also ends with a trailing comma and space.

findings.title: Multiple providers no longer rejected; ties resolved by arbitrary order
findings.detail: The previous guard for multiple providers was removed. With equal order values, such as the default, elytron and FIPS providers (all 200), the choice depends on classpath order. A misconfiguration that was previously caught now silently picks one provider.

findings.title: Test uses default EC key size for all three algorithms
findings.detail: The key pair is generated with the JDK default EC size, which is 256 bits, and then reused for ES256, ES384 and ES512 with signature lengths of 64, 96 and 132 bytes. The DER→concat→DER→concat round trip is therefore never exercised with real P-384 or P-521 signatures, so it cannot catch size-specific bugs such as length encoding above 127 bytes.

findings.title: Length check rejects valid long-form lengths and can mis-handle multi-byte tags
findings.detail: readLength() rejects any long-form length >= limit, where limit is the full input size. A valid DER value whose content length is close to the total buffer size can hit this check. readNext() also builds the element length from count, which includes tag and length bytes consumed by the sub-reads. The `-1` returned for indefinite length is later used as a byte count, so readSequence()/read() can throw NegativeArraySizeException or loop incorrectly instead of an IOException.
findings.evidence: if (length >= limit) // after all we must have read at least 1 byte

findings.title: readSequence ignores the declared length and can loop forever or read past the end
findings.detail: The loop `while (length > 0)` subtracts each element's size. With indefinite length (-1) the loop is skipped silently. Elements are not validated against the sequence content, and trailing data after the sequence is not checked. Malformed signatures can therefore be accepted or produce unexpected runtime exceptions instead of IOException.

findings.title: High tag number parsing does not handle EOF/negative values before checking
findings.detail: In readTagNumber, `(b & 0x7f) == 0` is evaluated when b == -1. -1 & 0x7f is 0x7f, which is non-zero, so the EOF is not caught by this check despite the comment saying it is. The following loop then falls through to the b < 0 check. The comment is misleading, and the shift/accumulate is not overflow-guarded.

findings.title: Unsupported crypto operations throw at runtime from a provider that is now selectable
findings.detail: Most CryptoProvider methods, such as getSignature, getX509CertFactory and getAlgorithmProvider, throw UnsupportedOperationException. CryptoIntegration.init in AuthzClient.create now picks whichever provider is on the classpath, so a missing full provider yields only runtime failures. Also getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the keystore's provider (typically SUN), which is not Bouncy Castle despite the method contract.

findings.title: Redundant dead encoder calls in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
findings.detail: The two ASN1Encoder.create().write(...) calls produce results that are discarded, and the integers are then encoded again. This is wasted work and looks like leftover debugging code.

findings.title: Non-constant format string passed to logger.debugf
findings.detail: The message built from class names is passed as the format string to debugf. A '%' in a class name would be interpreted as a format specifier. The message also ends with a trailing ', '.

findings.title: Grant type taken from raw form param can be spoofed or inconsistent

findings.title: Test for incorrect grant type catches any RuntimeException including AssertionError path

findings.title: Constructor dereferences formParams without null check and stores grant type that may be stale

findings.title: Grant type taken from request form parameter overrides actual grant

findings.title: Maps updated non-atomically in lazy refresh

findings.title: encodeTokenId throws for grant types without shortcut / unset grant type

findings.title: Context grantType taken from form params NPE-prone and not matching actual grant

findings.title: Wrong variable checked for null rawTokenId

findings.title: Duplicate-shortcut validation is ineffective

findings.title: Unused import added

findings.title: Reader thread is never joined, so the test is racy and may miss failures
findings.detail: The reader thread is started and never joined; the assertion on caughtExceptions runs right after deletedAll is set. An exception from the last in-flight request can be added after the assertion, and the thread can outlive the test and keep hitting the admin API during cleanup.

findings.title: Reader thread is a non-daemon thread with no failure handling
findings.detail: If the main thread fails during deletion (for example a remove() throws), deletedAll is never set. The non-daemon thread then loops forever and hangs the JVM or test run.

findings.title: getSubGroupsCount returns null when the group is concurrently deleted

findings.title: Test swallows the real failures into an unlogged list and ignores ordering of cleanup
findings.detail: The test creates 100 groups and deletes them without registering cleanup, so a failure mid-deletion leaves groups behind. The caught exceptions are only asserted as empty, which gives a poor failure message.

findings.title: Reader thread never joined; exceptions after assert can be missed
findings.detail: The background reader is started as a non-daemon thread and never joined. The test sets the flag and asserts immediately, so an exception thrown by the reader's in-flight call is not captured, and the thread can outlive the test and run against a cleaned-up realm.

findings.title: Reader thread may not run concurrently with deletes
findings.detail: The reader is started with no synchronization (such as a latch) to ensure it has begun reading before deletions start. The race the test targets may therefore not be exercised, and the test can pass without catching the bug.

findings.title: Test leaves admin events unpolled and uses 100 groups without event handling
findings.detail: The test creates and deletes 100 groups, generating 200 admin events (the realm has events enabled), and never skips or clears them. Later assertions in the same class that poll adminEvents may see stale events if the event queue is shared across tests.

findings.title: getSubGroupsCount returns null for a missing group
findings.detail: The Long return now silently yields null when the group was deleted. Callers such as GroupUtils.populateSubGroupCount pass it to setSubGroupCount and may NPE or emit a null count, where before they would get an error or a real count.

findings.title: Reader thread is never joined and may outlive the test
findings.detail: The reader thread is started but never joined. The test asserts caughtExceptions right after setting the flag, so an exception thrown by an in-flight request is missed. The thread can also still be running after the test ends and the realm is cleaned up, producing spurious failures in later tests.

findings.title: Created groups are not cleaned up and admin events are not drained
findings.detail: The test creates 100 groups and deletes them without consuming the generated admin events (adminEvents.poll/skipAll). Other tests in this class assert on events, so leftover events can break them. If the test fails midway, the created groups are not registered with cleanup either.

findings.title: Reader loop may not run between deletions or may hammer the server unboundedly
findings.detail: The reader thread loops with no pause and no guarantee of a request overlapping the deletions. The test is therefore flaky as a regression test for the race. Loading every group with Integer.MAX_VALUE in a tight loop is also heavy.

findings.title: getSubGroupsCount returns null for a deleted group
findings.detail: When the group was deleted concurrently, the method now returns null, a boxed Long. Callers such as GroupUtils.populateSubGroupCount pass it straight to setSubGroupCount, and other callers may unbox it, which can cause an NPE or a silently missing count. The other getSubGroupsStream methods in the class still dereference modelSupplier.get() directly, so a deleted group is handled inconsistently.

findings.title: Recovery codes stored in user storage as raw plaintext

findings.title: No fallback when the federated storage does not support recovery codes

findings.detail: The new Optional from getCredential is unwrapped with get(). If no credential is found (for example, federated credentials not matching), NoSuchElementException is thrown and the login page breaks.

findings.title: Federated credential model built without id/credential data, mismatching the validator
findings.detail: getCredentials rebuilds the recovery model from `createFromValues` using the raw codes, which hashes them and generates different data than what isValid compares. Also the stored id is not carried over, so removeStoredCredentialById on the model gets a different/null id.

findings.title: getCredentials NPEs when user is unknown
findings.detail: getMyUser can return null, as other methods in the same class explicitly check, but getCredentials dereferences myUser unconditionally.

findings.title: Recovery code validation compares raw code, ignores used codes, and is not constant-time
findings.detail: isValid accepts any code in the stored list every time, so codes are never consumed and can be replayed. It uses plain equals.

findings.title: Deserialization failure swallowed without exception details
findings.detail: IOException is caught and a message logged without the exception, hiding the cause and silently dropping the credential.

findings.title: supportsCredentialType NPE on null type and incomplete disable support
findings.detail: credentialType.equals is called on a possibly null argument, unlike the style used for PASSWORD. Also getDisableableCredentialTypesStream/disableCredentialType don't handle recovery codes though the type is now supported.
