findings.title: Storing raw recovery codes in user storage; no error on updateCredential
findings.detail: The raw (unhashed) recovery codes are serialized to JSON and passed to the federated user store via updateCredential, while the local DB path stores only hashes. The user storage receives and persists plaintext recovery codes, which is a weaker handling than the local path.

findings.title: Unchecked Optional.get() when no credential exists
findings.detail: getCredential can return an empty Optional (e.g. the federated stream lacks the credential and none is stored locally); calling get() throws NoSuchElementException and breaks the login page rendering instead of failing gracefully.

findings.title: Used-code state not persisted for federated credentials
findings.detail: After a successful validation, the credential is read from federated storage but allCodesUsed removal goes through removeStoredCredentialById, which only affects local DB. For federated credentials, the exhausted credential is never removed, and used-code tracking is not updated.

findings.title: Recovery code model rebuilt from raw codes loses ID and usage state
findings.detail: getCredentials recreates the model via createFromValues on each call, so the credential is never given the stored id and used-code state is never tracked. Each code can be reused indefinitely, and the displayed code number is always the first.

findings.title: Deserialization failure swallowed without exception detail
findings.detail: IOException is caught and logged with no exception or user information, hiding the cause and silently dropping the credential.
findings.evidence: log.error("Could not deserialize  credential of type: recovery-codes");

findings.title: getMyUser result dereferenced without null check
findings.detail: getMyUser may return null for users unknown to the map; myUser.recoveryCodes then throws NPE (other methods null-check).

findings.title: Typo in config alias
findings.detail: Alias 'delayed-suthenticator-config' is misspelled.

findings.title: Raw recovery codes sent to user storage but only hashed codes stored locally
findings.detail: The user storage receives the plaintext codes, while the local DB path stores hashed codes through the credentialModel. The two backends hold different representations. A user storage that persists the input can expose usable recovery codes.

findings.title: Unchecked Optional.get() when credential is missing
findings.detail: RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential returns an Optional, but get() is called without a presence check. Throws NoSuchElementException if no credential is found, for example when the federated provider returns nothing.

findings.title: getCredential can return a federated credential that is not locally removable
findings.detail: A federated credential is preferred. After all codes are used, the authenticator calls removeStoredCredentialById on the federated credential's id, which targets local storage and does nothing for the federated one. Exhausted federated codes are never removed or updated.

findings.title: Recovery code credential stored without creating a hashed model; used codes never tracked
findings.detail: The storage keeps a raw list of codes. isValid matches any code from the list and never marks it used or removes it, so codes are reusable. getCredentials also rebuilds the model from values without tracking consumed state.

findings.title: Plain equals against raw codes ignores input normalization/hash and NPE risks
findings.detail: The raw List is compared with key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse()) on an unchecked raw type. If the stored element types differ, or stored credential data is stored hashed, validation fails. The test only passes because the raw code is stored.

findings.title: supportsCredentialType may NPE on null type
findings.detail: credentialType.equals(...) is called on the possibly-null argument, whereas the existing branches use constant-first comparison.

findings.detail: Authenticator config alias is misspelled ('suthenticator').

findings.title: canManage() grants manage rights for a mere VIEW permission
findings.detail: canManage() calls hasPermission with both VIEW and MANAGE scopes, so an admin who only has view on groups passes the manage check. This lets a view-only admin create groups and requireManage() succeed, which is privilege escalation.

findings.title: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns resource IDs and evaluates by the wrong key
findings.detail: The resource's own ID is passed to hasPermission, which looks resources up by name, where the name is the group ID. The lookup therefore misses and falls back to the all-groups resource. The returned set also holds resource IDs rather than group IDs, so the user search filter by groups is wrong.

findings.title: switch on a possibly null resourceType throws NPE
findings.detail: The previous if/equals chain was null-safe. The new switch on resourceType throws NullPointerException if the type is null, instead of the intended error.

findings.title: requireManageMembers Javadoc references the wrong check
findings.detail: The Javadoc for requireManageMembers says it throws when canManageMembership returns false. The method concerns canManageMembers, so the documentation is misleading.

findings.title: canManage() grants manage-all-groups on VIEW-only permission
findings.detail: The no-arg canManage() accepts the VIEW scope as well as MANAGE. An admin who may only view all groups therefore passes requireManage() and can create top-level groups and perform other management operations.

findings.title: Resource IDs used where group IDs are expected in getGroupIdsWithViewPermission
findings.detail: In V2 the resource name is the group ID, but the resource ID is a separate UUID. The lambda passes groupResource.getId() to hasPermission, which looks it up by name, so it never matches and falls back to the all-groups resource. It also returns resource IDs as 'group IDs', and the type-level 'Groups' resource is included. The group filter used by user search is therefore wrong.

findings.title: Javadoc on requireManageMembers references wrong check
findings.detail: requireManageMembers(GroupModel) is documented as throwing when canManageMembership returns false. The evaluator class itself uses canManageMembers for this, so the documented contract does not match the method name.

findings.title: Javadoc says Stream but method returns Set
findings.detail: The @return tag for getGroupIdsWithViewPermission says 'Stream of IDs', but the method returns a Set<String>.
findings.evidence: * @return Stream of IDs of groups with view permission.

findings.title: canManage() on all groups is granted by the VIEW scope
findings.detail: GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() accepts the VIEW scope as well as MANAGE when checking the all-groups permission. An admin who can only view groups therefore passes requireManage() and can create, update and delete groups. Its own javadoc says canManage() requires MANAGE, so the VIEW scope should not be accepted.

findings.title: Resource UUID used instead of group id when collecting viewable groups
findings.detail: Group resources are named by the group id (see resolveGroup), but this code passes the resource's own id to hasPermission(), which looks the resource up by name. The lookup misses and falls back to the all-groups resource. The resource UUID, not the group id, is then added to the returned set. The all-groups type resource (name 'Groups') may also be returned. UserModel.GROUPS then receives wrong ids, so member-based user search by group permission is wrong.

findings.title: Group removal listener hits V2 method that throws UnsupportedOperationException
findings.detail: The GroupRemovedEvent listener calls groups().setPermissionsEnabled(group, false). With V2, groups() returns GroupPermissionsV2, whose setPermissionsEnabled always throws UnsupportedOperationException. Deleting any group when V2 is enabled will fail or abort the event processing.

findings.title: Javadoc of requireManageMembers references the wrong check
findings.detail: requireManageMembers is documented as throwing when canManageMembership returns false, but it should relate to canManageMembers. The getGroupIdsWithViewPermission javadoc also says it returns a Stream although the method returns a Set.

findings.title: Javadoc on void require* methods says they return true
findings.detail: requireView() and requireViewClientScopes() are void methods that throw ForbiddenException, but their Javadoc says "Returns true if ...". The docs contradict the signatures and the sibling require* docs.

findings.title: Clients resource type added without matching display-name handling
findings.detail: Per-client resources are named by the client's internal id, but getResourceName only maps USERS to a readable name. For CLIENTS it falls through to resource.getDisplayName(), which can be null or the raw UUID, so permission resources show no usable name.

findings.title: Removal listener disabled for V2, leaving orphaned client resources
findings.detail: The cleanup listener now runs only when the V1 feature is enabled. With V2 only, deleting a client does not remove its per-client authorization resource or permission references, so stale resources stay in the admin-permissions resource server.

findings.title: Cleanup listener gated on V1 flag; V2 + V1 together still hits unsupported calls
findings.detail: The listener runs only when the V1 feature is on. When V1 and V2 are both enabled, management() returns the V2 implementation, and its clients().setPermissionsEnabled throws UnsupportedOperationException, so removing a client or role can fail. When only V2 is enabled, nothing cleans up the per-client resources and permissions of a deleted client, leaving orphan data.

findings.title: getClientsWithPermission also returns the all-clients type resource
findings.detail: findByType returns every resource of type Clients, including the 'Clients' all-resource itself. If that resource is granted the scope, its name 'Clients' is added to the result alongside real client ids, so callers get a value that is not a client id.

findings.title: Possible NPE when the all-clients resource is missing
findings.detail: getResourceTypeResource can return null, for example if the schema is not supported or the resource is absent. The result is passed straight into findByResource, which dereferences it, instead of returning false.

findings.title: getResourceName not extended for the Clients resource type
findings.detail: Resources of type Clients are now created, but getResourceName only maps the Users type. Client resources fall back to getDisplayName, which is the internal client UUID, and the 'All clients' label is never produced.

findings.title: JUnit 4 fail() mixed into a JUnit 5 test, and create(null) used as a negative check
findings.detail: The test imports org.junit.Assert.fail instead of the JUnit 5 Assertions. testViewAllClients also calls clients().create(null) and expects 403, so a 400 or client-side error for the null body could mask or replace the permission check being tested.

findings.title: Possible NPE when the all-clients resource is missing

findings.title: JUnit 4 fail() used in a JUnit 5 test
findings.detail: The test imports org.junit.Assert.fail, which is JUnit 4, while the rest of the class and its sibling tests use JUnit 5 (org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.fail). This depends on a stray JUnit 4 dependency on the classpath.

findings.title: Test mutates shared client state without restoring it
findings.detail: testManageOnlyOneClient renames 'myclient' and removes then re-adds a default client scope as an optional scope. The @AfterEach only removes permissions, so later tests see the modified client.
